m1-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Open Google Colab and run Python in it without installing anything.
  • Create a private Edge Impulse project and find your way around its menu.
  • Connect your phone to Edge Impulse as a free accelerometer and microphone.
  • Prepare an Arduino Nano 33 BLE Sense or a micro:bit V2 if you own one, and fix the setup problems people hit most.

The Arduino Nano 33 BLE Sense is smaller than a stick of gum. It has 256 KB of RAM, less than a single photo from your phone, and yet it can hear a spoken word, feel a gesture, and react in a few milliseconds with no internet connection at all. Getting a model to fit in a space that small is what TinyML is about, and it's what this course teaches.

You don't need the board. Every lesson works with two free tools and the phone you probably already carry.

#Three tools, three jobs

  • Google Colab is a Jupyter notebook that runs on a Google computer and shows up in your browser. NumPy, scikit-learn, matplotlib, SciPy, and PyTorch come preinstalled. This is where you'll build windows, features, classifiers, and quantized models yourself, line by line.
  • Edge Impulse Studio is a web tool that does the same pipeline at production scale: it collects data from real sensors, extracts features, trains, estimates memory and latency for a chip, and builds the result for a device. Its Developer plan is free.
  • Your phone can join an Edge Impulse project as a sensor through its web browser, so you can record real motion and sound without any hardware.

#Step 1: Open Google Colab

  1. Go to colab.research.google.com (opens in a new tab) and sign in with a Google account.
  2. In the window that opens, choose New notebook. (If no window appears, use File › New notebook in Drive.)
  3. Click the name Untitled0.ipynb at the top left and rename it tinyml-setup.ipynb. Colab saves it in a folder called Colab Notebooks in your Google Drive.
  4. Click inside the first cell, type print("hello, edge"), and press Shift+Enter. The first run takes a few seconds while Colab connects you to a computer, and then the text appears under the cell.

Colab works the same on Windows, macOS, ChromeOS, and Linux, in Chrome, Edge, Firefox, or Safari. You'll run the real version check in the next lesson.

📝 Note

Some school Google accounts have Colab switched off by the school's administrator. If you see a message saying Colab isn't available for your account, use a personal Google account instead, or ask your teacher whether it can be turned on.

#Step 2: Create an Edge Impulse account and a private project

Edge Impulse's terms of service say account holders must be at least 18. If you're younger, ask a parent, guardian, or teacher to create the account and the project, then work in it together. If that isn't possible, skip the Edge Impulse parts: every lesson's Colab code teaches the same idea without it.

  1. Go to studio.edgeimpulse.com/signup (opens in a new tab) and sign up. Confirm the email address if asked.
  2. Create a new project and name it tinyml-course-motion. If you're asked whether it should be public or private, choose private. The free plan allows 3 private projects and unlimited public ones, and a public project shares all of its data with anyone.
  3. The project opens on its Dashboard.

The Developer plan gives each training job up to 60 minutes of compute, which is far more than any model in this course needs.

#Step 3: Tour the project menu

The menu on the left follows the order you'll build things in. You don't need to click everything now, but find each of these:

Menu item What happens there
Dashboard Project settings, collaborators, and the project ID
Devices Phones and boards connected to the project, with a green dot when online
Data acquisition Recording new samples and browsing your training and test data
Create impulse Choosing the window size, the feature extraction block, and the learning block
Live classification Sending new data from a device through your trained model
Model testing Running the model on the test set you held back
Deployment Building the model as an Arduino library, C++ code, firmware, or a phone app

Near the top of the page there's also a target device setting (it starts at a Cortex-M4F at 80 MHz). Studio uses it to estimate how much RAM, flash, and time your model would need on that chip, which becomes important in later modules.

#Step 4: Connect your phone as a sensor

  1. Open Devices and choose Connect a new device.
  2. Pick Mobile phone. A QR code appears.
  3. Scan it with your phone's camera and open the link. The page on your phone should say it's connected.
  4. Back on the Devices page, your phone is listed with a green dot.

When you record data later, the phone asks for permission to use its motion sensors or microphone. Allow it only while you're recording.

Then flash the Edge Impulse firmware and connect:

  1. Plug in the board and press RESET twice quickly. An LED on the board starts to pulse, which means the board is waiting for new firmware.
  2. Download the Edge Impulse firmware for this board (opens in a new tab), unzip it, and run the script for your system: flash_windows.bat, flash_mac.command, or flash_linux.sh.

#Optional: set up a micro:bit V2

The micro:bit isn't on Edge Impulse's list of supported boards, but the free micro:bit CreateAI (opens in a new tab) tool runs the same collect, train, and deploy loop for motion. It needs no account. Open it in Chrome or Edge on a laptop or Chromebook, connect the micro:bit over Bluetooth (or with a second micro:bit plugged in by USB as a radio link), record one-second samples of at least two actions, and train. You then code with the model in MakeCode and download it to the micro:bit, where it runs with no computer attached. Only a V2 can run the model.

#When something goes wrong

⚠️ Watch out

The phone connects, but Data acquisition records nothing (Chrome on Android). Chrome may be blocking motion sensors for the site. Open Chrome's Settings › Site settings › Motion sensors and allow them, then reload the page from the QR code.

⚠️ Watch out

edge-impulse-daemon can't find the board, or says the port is busy. Only one program can talk to the board's serial port at a time. Close the Arduino IDE's Serial Monitor and any other terminal running an Edge Impulse tool, unplug the board, plug it back in, and try again. If the computer never sees the board at all, swap the cable for one you know carries data.

⚠️ Watch out

bad CPU type in executable while flashing on an Apple silicon Mac. One of the flashing tools is built for Intel Macs and needs Rosetta 2. Install it with softwareupdate --install-rosetta --agree-to-license and run the flash script again.

⚠️ Watch out

npm install fails on Windows with a message about Visual Studio Build Tools. Part of the CLI is compiled during install. Re-run the Node.js installer with Tools for Native Modules ticked, then run the install command again in Command Prompt.

You're ready for the next lesson when a Colab cell prints text and Edge Impulse shows your phone under Devices with a green dot.

m1-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Confirm that Colab has every library the course uses.
  • Generate a synthetic three-axis accelerometer signal with NumPy and chart it.
  • Compute two features, mean and RMS, and see which one tells resting from shaking.
  • Train a scikit-learn model, measure its size in bytes, and compare it to a microcontroller's RAM.
  • Record a real 10-second motion sample from your phone in Edge Impulse.

By the end of this page you'll have done a miniature version of the whole course: sensor data in, features out, a trained model, and a check on whether it fits on a chip. It takes five short cells. Make a new Colab notebook called tinyml-first-run.ipynb, and paste each cell in as you go. Run them in order with Shift+Enter, because later cells use names that earlier cells create.

#Cell 1: prove the libraries are there

Your version numbers will differ from the ones shown here, since Colab updates its libraries every few months. What matters is that every line prints. If one line raises ModuleNotFoundError, the runtime didn't start properly: choose Runtime › Restart session and run the cell again.

#Cell 2: fake an accelerometer

An accelerometer reports acceleration along three axes, x, y, and z, usually in units of g (1 g is the pull of gravity). A board lying flat reads about 1 g on z and about 0 on x and y. Shake it and x and y swing back and forth.

Real sensors are coming. For now NumPy can produce a convincing fake: 3 seconds resting, then 3 seconds of shaking at 4 times per second, sampled 50 times per second, with a little random noise on every reading.

np.where(still, 0.0, ...) picks 0 for the resting half and the sine wave for the shaking half. The seed=1 makes the "random" noise identical every time you run the cell, which means your chart matches this one exactly.

#Cell 3: find a feature that separates the two halves

A model doesn't look at a chart. It needs a few numbers that summarize a stretch of signal. Those numbers are called features. Two simple ones:

  • Mean: the average value.
  • RMS (root mean square): square every value, average the squares, take the square root. It measures how big the signal is, whichever direction it points.

Before running the next cell, guess: which feature will look different for resting and shaking?

The means are both near zero. A sine wave spends as long below zero as above it, so its average cancels out. RMS squares the values first, so negative swings count as much as positive ones, and the shaking half comes out more than twenty times larger. Picking features that capture the thing you care about is half of TinyML, and Module 3 is built around it.

#Cell 4: train a tiny shake detector

Now make 40 short windows of 2 seconds each, half resting and half shaking at a random strength and speed, and train a decision tree that is allowed only one question.

The model is a single threshold: if the RMS is above a number somewhere between the resting and shaking values, call it shaking. That's a real model, trained from labeled data, and it predicts both new windows correctly. It's also small enough to be written in one line of C on a microcontroller.

#Cell 5: weigh the model

A microcontroller has two kinds of memory that matter: flash, where the program and model are stored, and RAM, the working memory used while it runs. The Nano 33 BLE Sense has 1 MB of flash and 256 KB of RAM. How big is the model we just trained?

pickle.dumps turns the Python object into bytes, so its length is a rough size. It overstates the true cost, because pickle also stores Python class names and bookkeeping that a chip would never need. On a microcontroller this model is one float and a comparison, about 4 bytes. Later modules measure models with tens of thousands of weights, where the size really does decide whether the model fits.

🧪 Try it yourself

In cell 4, change strength = rng.uniform(0.8, 2.0) to rng.uniform(0.02, 0.1), so the "shaking" is barely stronger than the noise. Run cells 4 and 5 again. Does the tree still separate the two classes, and how did its threshold move?

#Now record a real sample in Edge Impulse

Synthetic data is great for learning because you control everything. Real data is messier, so look at some now.

  1. In your Edge Impulse project, open Data acquisition. Your phone (connected in the last lesson) should be listed as a device.
  2. Under Record new data, set the label to shake, choose the accelerometer sensor, and set the sample length to 10000 ms (10 seconds).
  3. Click Start sampling, pick up your phone, and shake it gently from side to side until the recording ends.
  4. Click the new sample in the list. You'll see three lines, one per axis, just like the chart in cell 2.

Compare your real sample to the synthetic one. The real z axis probably isn't flat at 1 g, because you didn't hold the phone level. The shake isn't a perfect sine wave, and its strength drifts as your arm gets tired. Those differences are why the course mixes synthetic data, where you can see the idea clearly, with real data, where you find out whether the idea survives.

📝 Note

If you're working without an Edge Impulse account, you're still done with this lesson: cells 1 to 5 are the proof that your setup works.

#Check that everything is ready

  • Cell 1 printed a version for all five libraries.
  • Cell 2 drew a chart that is flat for 3 seconds, then wavy.
  • Cell 4 printed predictions [0 1].
  • Cell 5 printed a size in bytes.
  • Edge Impulse shows a 10-second shake sample with three axis lines (if you're using Edge Impulse).

Key takeaways

  • Colab comes with NumPy, scikit-learn, matplotlib, SciPy, and PyTorch; run cells top to bottom so names exist when you use them.
  • A feature is a number computed from a window of signal; RMS captures how big a motion is, while the mean of a back-and-forth motion is near zero.
  • A model's size in bytes decides whether it fits in a microcontroller's flash and RAM, and pickle gives only a rough upper bound.
  • Real sensor data drifts, tilts, and varies in ways a clean synthetic signal doesn't.

m1-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Explain the difference between a Colab notebook (kept in Drive) and its runtime (deleted when idle).
  • Organize the course's notebooks and data so you can rerun any lesson months later.
  • Decide what sensor data you may record, keep, and share, and set an Edge Impulse project up to match.
  • Handle a development board and its power safely.
  • Diagnose the Colab and Edge Impulse problems you're most likely to hit.

You train a model on Monday, close the laptop, and on Tuesday you open the same notebook and run the cell that tests it. Colab answers with this:

The code is still there. Your outputs from Monday are still printed under the cells. But the variables are gone, so the very first name Python looks up, model, doesn't exist. Once you know why, it takes five seconds to fix.

#The notebook is kept, the runtime is not

A Colab notebook has two halves. The notebook file lives in your Google Drive and keeps your code, your text, and the output each cell printed last time. The runtime is a temporary virtual machine that actually executes the code. It holds your variables and any files you created in /content. Colab deletes a runtime after it has been idle for a while, and on the free tier no runtime lasts more than 12 hours.

So the fix for Tuesday's NameError is Runtime › Run all, which rebuilds every variable in order. Get in the habit of choosing Runtime › Restart session and then Run all before you trust a result. It proves the notebook works from top to bottom, not just in the order you happened to click.

#Organize the course so you can rerun it

  • One notebook per lesson, named after it: m3-l2-gesture-windows.ipynb, m4-l2-keyword-int8.ipynb. Keep them together in one Drive folder called TinyML course (new notebooks land in Colab Notebooks, so drag them across in Google Drive).
  • Make data in code, not by hand. Every dataset in this course is generated by a cell or recorded in Edge Impulse, so rerunning the notebook recreates it.
  • Seed your randomness. Synthetic data uses NumPy's random generator. Give it a seed and the "random" numbers repeat exactly:

Without the seed, c is different every run, and so is any accuracy you compute from it. When you're comparing two versions of a model, a seed makes sure the only thing that changed is the thing you changed.

  • Save files you want to keep in Drive, not /content. A cell can connect your Drive to the runtime, after which anything saved under /content/drive/MyDrive survives:

Colab asks you to approve access the first time. For this course you rarely need it, because the data is regenerated by code.

  • Back up. File › Download › Download .ipynb saves a copy to your computer. In Edge Impulse, the Versioning page stores a snapshot of a project's data and settings that you can return to.

#Sensor data is personal data

It's easy to think of accelerometer numbers as harmless. They aren't always. The way a person walks is distinctive enough to identify them, a day of motion data shows when they sleep and leave the house, and a microphone records everyone in the room, not just the person who pressed Start sampling. Edge AI is often chosen because it can keep data like this on the device, a trade-off you'll measure in Module 7.

Four rules for this course:

  1. Record only yourself, or people who agreed first after you told them what you're recording and why.
  2. Keep Edge Impulse projects private. A public project publishes all of its data. Edge Impulse's terms also forbid content involving minors in public projects, so never make a project public if it holds recordings of anyone under 18.
  3. Label by class, not by person. Use labels like wave or idle, never someone's name.
  4. Delete what you don't need. When a project is finished, remove raw recordings of voices or faces you no longer use.

Sharing a Colab notebook shares its printed outputs too. If an output shows something you'd rather not share, use Edit › Notebook settings and tick Omit code cell output when saving this notebook before sharing.

#Handle boards safely

The Nano 33 BLE Sense and the micro:bit run on low voltages from USB and are safe to touch, but they can still be damaged, or damage things.

  • Power them from a computer USB port or a phone charger, through the board's own connector. Never connect a power supply directly to the pins unless a lesson's wiring diagram says exactly how.
  • Keep a bare board off metal surfaces, keys, and loose wires. The pins on the underside can short against metal and destroy the board.
  • Touch a grounded metal object before handling a board in dry weather, so a static spark doesn't hit the chip.
  • Treat lithium batteries with care if you use one later. Use a charger made for that battery, don't charge one unattended, and stop using any battery that swells, gets hot, or is dented.
  • Unplug before changing any wiring, and plug back in only after checking it.

#Make the tools work for you

Colab is fully usable from the keyboard. Shift+Enter runs a cell and moves to the next one, Ctrl+Enter (Cmd+Enter on a Mac) runs it and stays put, and Ctrl+M H shows the full list of shortcuts. Browser zoom (Ctrl and +) enlarges both code and charts.

Every chart in this course has a text description, and the lessons print the key numbers next to each chart so nothing depends on color alone. When you draw your own charts, give each line a different style as well as a different color (linestyle="--"), or switch to a palette designed for color-vision deficiency with plt.style.use("tableau-colorblind10").

#Getting unstuck

What you see What it means What to do
NameError: name 'x' is not defined The cell that creates x hasn't run in this session Runtime › Run all
A cell shows a spinning icon for minutes A loop is too slow or never ends Runtime › Interrupt execution, then shrink the data or fix the loop
"Your session crashed after using all available RAM" An array got far bigger than intended Check the shape of your arrays; a window count in the millions is usually a stride of 1 by mistake
ModuleNotFoundError for a course library The runtime didn't start cleanly Runtime › Restart session, then run again
Phone shows as offline in Devices The phone's screen locked or the tab closed Unlock it and reopen the page from the QR code
Edge Impulse job fails or stops A training run hit an error or the job time limit Read the job log at the bottom of the page; reduce the training cycles and try again

💡 Tip

When you ask for help, in a forum or from a teacher, include three things: the last line of the error, the cell that produced it, and what you expected to happen. Most problems get solved from those three alone.

m2-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Explain the difference between edge inference, cloud inference, and a cascade that uses both.
  • Calculate cloud and on-device latency for a payload, including upload time.
  • Calculate how much raw data a sensor produces per day and compare it with sending only decisions.
  • Estimate how radio use changes battery life, using stated assumptions.
  • Apply a decision flow that weighs latency, bandwidth, privacy, power, cost, and connectivity.

A phone's microphone produces 16,000 numbers every second. Apple's description of "Hey Siri" starts there: the phone turns your voice into "a stream of instantaneous waveform samples, at a rate of 16000 per second." If the phone shipped all of that to a server just to check for two words, it would upload gigabytes a day, mostly the sound of a quiet room, and keep its radio awake the whole time.

So it doesn't. A small neural network runs on a low-power processor inside the phone and listens for the trigger phrase. Only when it fires does the phone wake its main processor, check again with a bigger model, and finally send your request to Apple's servers, where the heavy speech recognition happens. That design, a tiny model on the device deciding when to call a big model in the cloud, is a pattern you'll meet again and again in edge AI. To choose it (or not) for your own device, you need numbers.

#Two places to run the same model

Inference means using a trained model to make a prediction. (Training usually happens on a big computer either way.) The question here is where inference happens.

  • Edge inference: the model runs on the device that holds the sensor. Only the decision, if anything, leaves.
  • Cloud inference: the device sends raw data (or features) to a server, which runs the model and sends an answer back.
  • Cascade: a small edge model filters the stream and wakes a larger cloud model only for the moments that matter. Wake words work this way.

Six factors decide between them. Three of them you can calculate directly, so start there.

#Latency: count the whole round trip

On a device, latency is roughly the time the model takes to run. In the cloud you also pay to upload the data, wait for the network round trip, and wait for the server. Upload time is the one people forget, and it grows with the payload:

upload time = bytes × 8 ÷ link speed in bits per second

The link speeds and timings are typical round numbers, not measurements, so change them and rerun. Notice what they show. For the 1,200-byte motion window, the cloud is slower but still under a tenth of a second, which is fine for most jobs. For a 2 MB photo on a slow rural link, upload alone takes 32 seconds, while a small image model on the camera answers in under one. Payload size times link speed usually decides latency, not how fast the server is.

#Bandwidth: raw sensor data adds up

A sensor that streams produces data every second of every day. Multiply it out:

A microphone streams about 2.8 GB a day. Sending 50 short event messages instead ("door knock at 14:02") costs about a kilobyte, roughly a million times less. Bandwidth costs money on a cellular plan, and on some links it's simply not available: long-range radios like LoRa carry messages of tens to a few hundred bytes, a few times an hour. A wildlife camera on that kind of link can't send photos, only counts like "3 deer, 1 fox".

#Power: the radio is the expensive part

On a battery device, sending data usually costs far more energy than computing on it, because a radio has to stay powered while it connects and transmits. The next cell compares streaming everything with deciding on the device. Every number in assume is a rough, typical value, not a datasheet figure, and the point is the ratio.

The edge version runs its model twice a second and still lasts months, because the microcontroller works for 20 ms and then sleeps, and the radio wakes only five times a day. Streaming keeps the radio on, so the same battery is flat before the end of a school day. Module 7 measures this properly with duty cycles.

#Privacy, cost, and connectivity

The last three factors are harder to put in one formula, but just as decisive.

Privacy. Data that never leaves the device can't leak in transit, can't be breached on a server, and can't be reused for something you didn't agree to. A smart doorbell that sends "person at door" reveals much less than one that streams video. Edge isn't automatically private, though: a stolen device still holds whatever it stored, and a firmware update can change what gets sent. The real principle is send the least data that does the job.

Cost. Cloud inference has a running cost per prediction, multiplied by every device, every day, for as long as the product exists. Edge inference moves the cost into the hardware: a chip with enough memory, and the engineering time to make the model fit.

Connectivity. Some devices have to work where there's no signal. Apple's fall detection is a good example: the watch detects the hard fall and starts the alert itself, and needs a cellular, Wi-Fi, or satellite link only to place the emergency call. A fall detector that needed the cloud to notice the fall would fail in a basement or on a hiking trail.

The cloud's big advantage is size. A server can run a model thousands of times larger than any microcontroller can hold, and you can update it without touching a single device.

#A decision flow you can reuse

Here's the same logic as a function, with one addition: if something forces the edge but the model doesn't fit, the answer isn't "cloud", it's "make the model smaller", which is what Modules 4 and 5 teach. Step through it for a fall detector that must work offline.

The 95 ms cloud latency easily meets a 1-second deadline, so latency adds no reason. The single reason is connectivity, and it's enough.

#Mistakes that flip the answer

⚠️ Watch out

Mixing up bits and bytes. Link speeds are quoted in bits per second (Mbit/s), file sizes in bytes. Forget the × 8 and every upload looks eight times faster than it is:

An answer of 4 seconds might pass a design review that 32 seconds would fail.

⚠️ Watch out

Planning with the average network instead of the worst one. A 70 ms round trip is typical on a good connection, but phones on a weak signal see seconds, and sometimes no connection at all. If missing a deadline is dangerous, design for the bad case.

⚠️ Watch out

Treating "edge" as free. The model still has to fit in the device's flash and RAM and run fast enough on its processor. A 50 MB model can't move onto a chip with 1 MB of flash just because the privacy argument is good.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1A doorbell sends a 150 KB photo whenever it sees motion, over a 2 Mbit/s uplink with an 80 ms round trip and 50 ms of server time. About how long until the answer comes back?

  • That counts the round trip and the server but leaves out the upload, which is the biggest part.

  • This treats 150 KB as 150,000 bits. Bytes must be multiplied by 8 first.

  • 150,000 × 8 = 1.2 million bits, which takes 600 ms at 2 Mbit/s; add 80 ms and 50 ms.

Show answer

C. 150,000 × 8 = 1.2 million bits, which takes 600 ms at 2 Mbit/s; add 80 ms and 50 ms.

2A voice assistant must answer open-ended questions, but you don't want everything the microphone hears sent to a server. Which design fits?

  • Encryption protects data on the way, but the server still receives every sound in the room.

  • The cascade keeps ordinary room audio local while still letting a big cloud model handle real questions.

  • A model that answers open-ended questions is far too large for a microcontroller's memory.

Show answer

B. The cascade keeps ordinary room audio local while still letting a big cloud model handle real questions.

3A sensor in a factory has wired power and Ethernet, reports once a minute, has no deadline tighter than a minute, and needs a 50 MB model. Where should it run?

  • Nothing here needs the edge, and the model wouldn't fit on a small device anyway.

  • It has a reliable link, plenty of time, and a model too big for a microcontroller, so nothing forces it onto the device.

  • Shrinking is the answer only when something forces edge inference, and nothing does here.

Show answer

B. It has a reliable link, plenty of time, and a model too big for a microcontroller, so nothing forces it onto the device.

4In the battery cell, why does streaming drain the battery so much faster even though the cloud does all the computing?

  • The server's power comes from the data center, not from the device's battery.

  • Running the model costs 15 mW for 20 ms at a time; the radio costs 500 mW for as long as it's on.

  • The model's size isn't the issue; the energy goes into transmitting data.

Show answer

B. Running the model costs 15 mW for 20 ms at a time; the radio costs 500 mW for as long as it's on.

Key takeaways

  • Edge inference runs the model next to the sensor; cloud inference sends data to a server; a cascade uses a small edge model to decide when to call a big cloud one.
  • Cloud latency = upload (bytes × 8 ÷ bit rate) + round trip + server time, and the upload often dominates.
  • Raw sensors produce megabytes to gigabytes a day; sending only decisions can cut that a millionfold.
  • On batteries the radio usually costs more energy than the computing, so deciding locally can stretch battery life from hours to months.
  • Privacy, running cost, and offline operation often settle the question even when latency doesn't, and a model that doesn't fit has to be made smaller, not wished onto the device.

#Further reading

What you'll learn

  • Turn a product idea into a small set of numbers a calculation can use.
  • Compute latency, daily data volume, link capacity, battery life, and cloud cost for each product.
  • Write a recommend() function that returns a verdict and the reasons for it.
  • Change one assumption and see which verdicts move.

Design reviews for connected devices tend to go in circles. One person says "the cloud is simpler," another says "edge is more private," and nobody has a number. This build ends the argument with a calculator. You'll describe three products as Python dictionaries, run five calculations on each, and get a report like this one, every line of which comes from code you write:

Open a new Colab notebook called m2-l2-edge-or-cloud.ipynb and add each cell as you go.

#Step 1: Describe each product as numbers

Every number below is a stated assumption, chosen to be realistic in size. That's the honest way to do early design: write the assumption down where everyone can see it and change it.

Where the numbers come from:

  • The speaker hears 16 kHz audio at 2 bytes a sample (32,000 B/s), checks a 1-second window four times a second, sits on home Wi-Fi, and is plugged into the wall (battery_wh=None).
  • The pendant samples a 3-axis accelerometer at 100 Hz, 2 bytes per reading (600 B/s), checks a 2-second window twice a second, and has a small 1.1 Wh battery. It must catch a fall in a basement with no signal, so offline_needed=True.
  • The camera takes a 50 KB photo every 10 seconds (5,000 B/s on average) and talks over a long-range, low-power radio of about 5 kbit/s. Its photos sometimes show hikers, so they count as sensitive.

#Step 2: Latency for each product

Reuse the formula from the Notes: upload, plus round trip, plus server time.

Only the camera misses its deadline in the cloud, and by a lot: one 50 KB photo takes 80 seconds to squeeze through a 5 kbit/s radio. The speaker and the pendant could both use the cloud on latency alone. That's worth knowing, because it means their verdicts will be decided by something else.

#Step 3: Data per day, and whether the link can carry it

A link has a fixed capacity per day. If the raw stream is bigger, streaming isn't slow, it's impossible.

The camera produces 432 MB a day and its radio can carry 54 MB, so the raw photos physically can't all be sent. For the speaker and pendant the link is hundreds of times bigger than needed, so bandwidth doesn't decide them either.

#Step 4: Battery life

The energy model from the Notes, with one improvement: each product's sensor has its own power draw, and a camera sensor uses much more than an accelerometer.

busy is the fraction of each second the processor spends running the model. The pendant computes for 15 ms twice a second, so it's busy 3% of the time and asleep the rest. Streaming would flatten its battery in about two hours. These figures count only sensing, computing, and the radio; a real product also powers a screen, lights, or a buzzer.

#Step 5: The cloud bill

Cloud prices vary, so PRICE_PER_MILLION is a made-up round number. Swap in a real quote when you have one. The comparison that matters is between calling the cloud on every window and calling it only on events.

Four checks a second, on ten thousand speakers, is about a hundred billion predictions a month. Sending only the 20 moments a day when someone actually says the wake word cuts that to six million.

#Step 6: Turn the numbers into a verdict

Now combine everything. The function collects a reason for each factor that pushes toward the device. Then it decides:

  • no reasons: either location works, so compare cost;
  • reasons, but the model is too big: shrink the model (we keep half the flash free for the rest of the firmware);
  • reasons that make the cloud impossible (offline, deadline, link too small): edge;
  • reasons that only make the cloud undesirable (sensitivity, battery): a cascade.

The speaker gets a cascade for a single reason, privacy, which matches what real smart speakers do. The pendant and the camera both land on the edge, but for different reasons: the pendant because it must work offline (and its battery agrees), the camera because its link and its deadline both rule out the cloud.

🧪 Try it yourself

Give the camera a cellular modem instead of the long-range radio: set link_mbps=5 and round_trip_ms=80, then rerun steps 2 to 6. Which reasons disappear, and does the verdict change?

#The finished calculator

Here's the whole thing in one cell, with a cost line added to the report. Paste it into a fresh notebook and it runs on its own.

📝 Note

The device_ms values here are guesses. Once a model is trained in Edge Impulse, the Studio estimates its processing time, RAM, and flash on the target device you chose, and those estimates are what you'd paste in. Module 5 does exactly that.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1The speaker's cloud latency (73 ms) beats its 300 ms deadline and its link is huge. Why does the calculator still not say "cloud"?

  • The speaker is plugged in; battery_days returns None for it.

  • Privacy is the one reason on its list, and it makes the cloud undesirable rather than impossible, which is exactly when a cascade fits.

  • An 80 KB model fits easily in 1 MB of flash, even with half kept free.

Show answer

B. Privacy is the one reason on its list, and it makes the cloud undesirable rather than impossible, which is exactly when a cascade fits.

2Why does recommend() treat "must work offline" differently from "raw data is sensitive"?

  • A device with no connection can't call the cloud at all, but a sensitive device can still call it for the rare moments that need it.

  • Plenty of offline devices are plugged in; the rule is about whether the cloud can be reached.

  • The function doesn't rank importance; it asks whether the cloud is possible at all.

Show answer

A. A device with no connection can't call the cloud at all, but a sensitive device can still call it for the rare moments that need it.

3The camera's model grows to 1,500 KB. What does the calculator now say?

  • The camera's link and deadline still rule out the cloud, so the model can't just move there.

  • It has reasons to run on the device but the model is more than half of its 2,048 KB flash, so the answer is to make it smaller.

  • The size check happens before the edge verdict, and 1,500 KB fails it.

Show answer

B. It has reasons to run on the device but the model is more than half of its 2,048 KB flash, so the answer is to make it smaller.

Key takeaways

  • Write every assumption as a named number; a design argument becomes a calculation anyone can rerun.
  • Latency, link capacity, and battery life are separate checks, and a product can pass one and fail another.
  • Separate the reasons that make the cloud impossible (offline, deadline, link) from the ones that make it undesirable (privacy, energy); the second kind points to a cascade.
  • Calling the cloud only on events, not on every window, cuts the cost and the data by orders of magnitude.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Add a fourth product of your own, such as a bike crash sensor, a baby monitor, or a beehive weight scale, and check whether the verdict matches your intuition.
  • Add a monthly_data_cost using a per-megabyte price for cellular data, and include it in the report.
  • Replace the fixed EVENT_BYTES with a field per product, so a camera that sends a small thumbnail with each event can be compared with one that sends only a count.

  • Use Fall Detection with Apple Watch (opens in a new tab), Apple Support: how a real fall detector behaves, including what happens when there's no cellular or Wi-Fi connection.

m2-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Calculate data rates and daily volumes for sensors you haven't seen yet.
  • Test a design against a latency deadline, including the worst-case network.
  • Work out how a cascade's false-positive rate changes the data it sends.
  • Compare battery life across three designs and pick the one that meets a target.
  • Find unit bugs, strip a payload down to what it needs, and pack a report into bytes.

These problems use new devices, not the three from the build. Write your answer in a Colab cell before opening the solution. The cells share variables, so run the warm-up first.

#Warm-up

A gyroscope measures rotation on 3 axes. At 200 readings per second with 2 bytes per reading, how many bytes per second does it produce?

Rate × channels × bytes per sample. Every data-rate question in this set starts from that product.

#Exercise 1: Three new sensors

Write bytes_per_day(rate_hz, channels, bytes_per_sample) and use it for a 25 Hz heart-rate sensor (1 channel, 2 bytes), stereo music at 44.1 kHz (2 channels, 2 bytes), and a 96 × 96 grayscale camera at 5 frames per second (each pixel is 1 byte, so treat every pixel as a channel). Print MB per day.

Need a hint?

A camera frame is 96 × 96 = 9,216 values at once. With channels=96 * 96 and rate_hz=5, the same formula works for images.

Show solution

The heart-rate sensor is small enough to stream all day over almost any link. Music and video are thousands of times bigger, which is why devices that listen or look usually decide locally.

#Exercise 2: A drone's 50 ms deadline

A small drone must react to an obstacle within 50 ms. Each decision needs one 96 × 96 grayscale frame. On a good day the drone has a 10 Mbit/s uplink with a 40 ms round trip, and the server needs 5 ms. Can the cloud meet the deadline? What about when the round trip rises to 200 ms?

Need a hint?

The payload is 9,216 bytes. Convert to bits before dividing by the link speed, then add the round trip and the server time.

Show solution

Even the good case misses by a couple of milliseconds, and the bad case misses by four times the deadline. A design that "almost" works on the average network fails exactly when the drone flies somewhere with a weak signal.

#Exercise 3: Sort five products

Write verdict(offline, cloud_in_time, link_big_enough, sensitive) that returns "edge" if the cloud is impossible, "cascade" if it's possible but the data is sensitive, and "cloud" otherwise. Then decide the four inputs for each product yourself and run it:

  • noise-cancelling earbuds (they must react to sound in under a millisecond or two)
  • a phone app that identifies plant diseases when the user taps Check
  • a voice-controlled light switch
  • a trail camera counting animals over a tiny radio link
  • an avalanche beacon that must work far from any signal
Need a hint?

"Cloud impossible" means any one of: it must work offline, the cloud misses the deadline, or the link can't carry the data. Check those three first, then sensitivity.

Show solution

The plant app is the one product where the cloud is the natural fit: a user taps a button, waits a second, and gets an answer from a model far bigger than a phone could hold comfortably. The earbuds are the opposite: no network on Earth answers in a millisecond.

#Exercise 4: The hidden cost of false alarms

A doorbell checks a camera frame twice a second for a person. Streaming every frame (30 KB each) would be expensive, so you design a cascade: an on-device person detector, and a 150 KB photo uploaded only when it fires. About 40 real visitors come per day. But the detector also fires falsely on some frames. Compare the MB uploaded per day for a false-positive rate of 2% per frame and 0.1% per frame, against streaming every frame.

Need a hint?

Frames per day = 2 × 86,400. False uploads = rate × frames per day. Total uploads = real visitors + false uploads.

Show solution

At 2%, false alarms outnumber real visitors 86 to 1. The cascade still beats streaming tenfold, but the edge model's false-positive rate, not the visitors, sets the data bill. A 2% error rate sounds small until you multiply it by 172,800 frames a day.

#Exercise 5: Will the pendant last a month?

A fall-detection pendant has a 150 mAh, 3.7 V battery and must last 30 days. It always draws 0.3 mW for the sensor and sleep. Compare three designs, using a 500 mW radio and a 15 mW processor that's busy 3% of the time when it runs a model:

  1. stream everything (radio always on)
  2. decide on the device, and send about 2 one-second messages a day
  3. decide on the device, but also send a 1-second "double-check" to the cloud every minute

Which designs meet the target?

Need a hint?

Energy in the battery: 0.150 Ah × 3.7 V × 3600 = joules. A radio on for 1 second, n times a day, averages 500 × n / 86,400 mW.

Show solution

Design 3 looks harmless, since it still decides on the device, but 1,440 radio wake-ups a day multiply its average power by twelve. Only design 2 survives the month, and only just, so the real product would need a bigger battery or fewer messages.

#Exercise 6: Find the unit bug

This function is supposed to return how many seconds a file takes to upload. For a 500 KB file on a 2 Mbit/s link it returns 250. Find the bug and fix it.

Need a hint?

Write out the units: KB ÷ (Mbit/s). What do you need to multiply KB by to get bits, and Mbit/s by to get bits per second?

Show solution

500 KB is 4 million bits, and a 2 Mbit/s link moves 2 million bits per second, so it takes 2 seconds. The buggy version was off by a factor of 125 (1,000,000 ÷ 8,000), and it never crashed or printed a warning. Unit bugs are dangerous precisely because the result looks like a normal number.

#Exercise 7: Send only what the cloud needs

A glass-break detector builds this event when it fires. The cloud only needs to know what happened, how sure the model was, and roughly when. Write minimize(event) that keeps the label, the confidence rounded to 2 decimals, and the time cut to the hour, and compare the sizes as JSON.

Need a hint?

The time is a string, so slicing it with [:13] keeps "2026-11-16T14".

Show solution

The audio, the exact location, and the owner's name were 99.9% of the bytes and 100% of the privacy risk. Dropping them doesn't stop the cloud from doing its job (logging alarms and notifying someone), which is the test for whether a field belongs in the message at all.

#Challenge: A 7-byte wildlife report

A camera in a forest counts animals on the device and reports over a long-range radio link. Some of these links allow as little as 11 bytes per message. Each report needs the counts of deer, fox, boar, and people (each 0 to 255), the battery percentage (0 to 100), and the time as minutes since midnight (0 to 1439).

Use Python's struct module to pack a report into as few bytes as possible, print it as hex, and unpack it again to prove nothing was lost.

Need a hint?

struct.pack("<B", n) stores one unsigned byte (0 to 255). Minutes since midnight can reach 1439, which doesn't fit in a byte, so use "H" (2 bytes, 0 to 65,535) for that field. "<" fixes the byte order and removes padding.

Show solution

Five 1-byte fields and one 2-byte field make 7 bytes, small enough for the tightest links. Compare that with the 50 KB photo the camera took: the report is about 7,000 times smaller and reveals nothing about any hiker beyond "2 people passed".

m3-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Choose a sampling rate high enough to capture a motion, and recognize aliasing when it's too low.
  • Cut a stream into windows with a chosen size and stride, and predict how many windows you'll get.
  • Label windows that contain one activity, and handle the ones that straddle a change.
  • Compute mean, standard deviation, RMS, and dominant frequency for each axis of a window.
  • Decide whether a problem is classification, anomaly detection, or regression.

A phone in someone's pocket records 20 seconds of accelerometer data: walking, then standing still, then walking again. At 50 readings per second on three axes, that's a 1,000 × 3 array. A classifier wants something quite different: lots of examples, each the same size, each with one label. The stream has no examples in it. It's one long recording with no boundaries.

Turning a stream into examples is the first real design decision in any sensor model. Get it wrong and no amount of training fixes it. This lesson covers the four choices involved: how often to sample, how to cut, how to label, and what to compute from each piece.

#Sampling rate: look often enough, or the signal lies

The sampling rate is how many readings per second the sensor takes. Too few and you miss the motion. Worse, you can see a motion that isn't there. Run this and look at the squares:

Sampled at 8 Hz, a 6 Hz shake looks exactly like a 2 Hz sway. This is aliasing, and no model can undo it, because the 8 Hz samples genuinely are identical to those of a 2 Hz wave.

The rule (the Nyquist criterion): the sampling rate must be more than twice the highest frequency you need to capture. In practice engineers leave a margin and sample 3 to 5 times faster. Human movement mostly sits below about 15 Hz, which is why motion projects commonly sample at 50 to 100 Hz (Edge Impulse's motion tutorial uses 62.5 Hz). Speech carries useful detail up to about 8 kHz, which is why keyword spotters sample at 16 kHz.

#Windows: fixed-size slices of the stream

A window is a slice of consecutive readings, and every window is the same length. Two numbers define how you cut:

  • window size W: how many samples (or seconds) each window holds.
  • stride S: how far the start moves between one window and the next. Edge Impulse calls this the window increase.

When the stride is smaller than the window, windows overlap. For a stream of N samples:

number of windows = ⌊(N − W) ÷ S⌋ + 1 overlap = 1 − S ÷ W

Before you step through the next program, use the formula to predict how many windows it makes from 8 numbers with W = 4 and S = 2.

(8 − 4) ÷ 2 + 1 = 3 windows, each sharing half its samples with the next. Now the real stream: 20 seconds at 50 Hz, cut into 2-second windows (100 samples) with a 1-second stride (50 samples).

The array shape (19, 100, 3) reads as 19 windows, 100 time steps, 3 axes. Each window is now one example.

How do you choose the numbers? The window size must be long enough to contain at least one full cycle of the slowest pattern you care about. One walking step takes about half a second, and the side-to-side sway repeats once every two steps, so a 2-second window holds a couple of complete cycles. The stride trades work for responsiveness: a smaller stride gives more training windows from the same recording and lets the device react sooner, but it means running the model more often.

#Labeling a window

Each sample has a label, but each window needs exactly one. When a window sits inside a single activity, that's easy. When it straddles a change, it isn't:

The window that starts at 7 seconds is half walking and half standing, so its "majority" label is a coin toss. Training on it teaches the model a contradiction. Common fixes: drop windows below a purity threshold (say 80%), or use the label at the end of the window, which is what a live device cares about ("what is happening now?"). Edge Impulse offers that second option for samples with several labels.

#Features: from 300 numbers to 12

A 2-second window holds 300 numbers. Small models do far better with a handful of numbers that describe what matters. For each axis, compute:

  • mean: the average, which mostly reflects how the device is tilted relative to gravity;
  • standard deviation and RMS: how much it moves;
  • dominant frequency: the strongest repeating rate, found with a Fourier transform (np.fft.rfft).

Walking has a z standard deviation more than ten times higher than standing, and a peak at 2.0 Hz. Two details are worth noticing. First, the frequency resolution is 50 ÷ 100 = 0.5 Hz, so a 1.8 Hz step rate shows up in the 2.0 Hz bin; longer windows give finer resolution. Second, the "peak" while standing is a random number, because the strongest frequency in pure noise means nothing. That's why a peak frequency should always travel with a measure of strength like the standard deviation.

Edge Impulse's Spectral Analysis block computes this kind of feature set (statistics plus frequency-domain power) for every window, and next lesson you'll build the same thing yourself.

#Three task types, one stream

Windows and features are the same whatever you ask the model. What changes is the question:

  • Classification picks one label from a list you defined: walk, stand, wave. Every class needs labeled examples.
  • Regression predicts a number: steps per minute, a machine's speed, how full a bin is.
  • Anomaly detection answers "is this unusual?" It's trained only on normal data, because the faults you most want to catch are rare and hard to record. A motor that has never failed can still learn what healthy vibration looks like.

The same ideas apply to images, except the window is spatial instead of temporal: one camera frame is one example, usually resized to something small like 96 × 96 pixels before it reaches the model.

#Mistakes that wreck sensor models

⚠️ Watch out

Leaking overlapping windows into the test set. With a 50% overlap, neighboring windows share half their samples. If you shuffle all windows and split randomly, the test set is full of near-copies of training windows, and accuracy looks far better than it will on a new person or a new day. Split by recording (or by person), so every window from one recording lands on the same side. Edge Impulse's dataset split settings can group samples by metadata for the same reason.

⚠️ Watch out

Training at one sampling rate and deploying at another. A phone might record at 100 Hz while the board runs at 62.5 Hz. A window of "100 samples" then covers a different amount of time, and the dominant-frequency feature shifts. Resample the training data to the device's rate, or set the rate explicitly in the impulse.

⚠️ Watch out

A stride of 1 on long recordings. It looks like free data, but it creates almost-identical windows: an hour at 100 Hz with a 2-second window gives about 360,000 windows that mostly repeat each other. Training slows down and the model gains little.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1A stream has 1,000 samples. You use windows of 200 samples with a stride of 100. How many windows do you get?

  • That would be windows that don't overlap (stride 200). A stride of 100 starts a new window twice as often.

  • (1000 − 200) ÷ 100 + 1 = 9. The last window starts at sample 800 and ends exactly at 1,000.

  • A window starting at sample 900 would need samples up to 1,100, which don't exist.

Show answer

B. (1000 − 200) ÷ 100 + 1 = 9. The last window starts at sample 800 and ends exactly at 1,000.

2A machine vibrates at 40 Hz when it's healthy. Which sampling rate is the lowest that won't alias it?

  • Sampling at exactly the vibration's frequency catches it at the same point every cycle, so it looks like a constant.

  • 60 Hz is below twice 40 Hz, so a 40 Hz vibration would alias to 20 Hz.

  • It's more than twice 40 Hz, with some margin, so the vibration's true frequency survives.

Show answer

C. It's more than twice 40 Hz, with some margin, so the vibration's true frequency survives.

3You split 2,000 overlapping windows from 10 recordings randomly into train and test, and get 99% accuracy. On a new recording the model scores 78%. What's the most likely cause?

  • Neighboring windows share samples, so a random split tests on near-copies of training windows.

  • More training would make it fit the training recordings even more closely, not generalize better.

  • Window length affects what patterns fit, but it doesn't explain a big gap between test and new data.

Show answer

A. Neighboring windows share samples, so a random split tests on near-copies of training windows.

4You want a model that warns when a fridge compressor starts sounding unusual, but you only have recordings of it working normally. Which task type fits?

  • You have no faulty examples to learn that class from.

  • It learns what normal looks like and flags anything far from it, so it needs only normal data.

  • Regression predicts a number, such as a temperature; it doesn't flag unusual behavior by itself.

Show answer

B. It learns what normal looks like and flags anything far from it, so it needs only normal data.

Key takeaways

  • Sample at more than twice the highest frequency you need (3 to 5 times in practice), or aliasing invents frequencies that aren't there.
  • Windows turn a stream into examples: W sets how much each example sees, S sets how many you get and how often the device decides; count = ⌊(N − W) ÷ S⌋ + 1.
  • Give every window one label, and drop or relabel windows that straddle a change.
  • Mean, standard deviation, RMS, and dominant frequency per axis turn hundreds of raw numbers into a dozen useful ones.
  • Classification picks a label, regression predicts a number, and anomaly detection learns normal and flags the rest.
  • Split overlapping windows by recording, never randomly.

#Further reading

  • Impulse design (opens in a new tab), Edge Impulse: the window size, window increase, frequency, and zero-pad settings, with a sketch of how windows slide.
  • Spectral analysis block (opens in a new tab), Edge Impulse: exactly which statistical and frequency features the Studio computes for motion data.
  • Cross-validation: GroupKFold (opens in a new tab), scikit-learn: how to keep every window from one recording on the same side of a split.

What you'll learn

  • Generate realistic synthetic accelerometer recordings, including the tilt and noise of a real hand.
  • Cut every recording into labeled windows while tracking which recording each window came from.
  • Extract 15 time and frequency features per window, and look at them the way Edge Impulse's feature explorer does.
  • Split by recording, train three classifiers, and compare their accuracy against their size.
  • Read a confusion matrix and set up the same pipeline in Edge Impulse Studio.

A gesture-controlled light switch needs to tell four things apart: the hand is still, it waves side to side, it moves up and down, or it draws a circle. By the end of this build you'll have a model that does that from accelerometer data, and you'll know exactly how big it is. The pipeline:

And the result you're building toward, a comparison where the smallest good model wins:

Make a Colab notebook called m3-l2-gesture-windows.ipynb.

#Step 1: Generate the recordings

Real recordings are coming in Step 7. Synthetic ones let you see every decision clearly, but they have to be realistic enough to be hard. Three things make them so:

  • every recording has its own speed and size of motion, like different people;
  • every recording is rotated by up to 30°, because nobody holds a device perfectly level, and rotation leaks motion from one axis into the others;
  • every reading gets noise.

Look at idle: x sits near −0.3 and y near +0.4 even though the hand isn't moving. That's gravity, split across the axes by the tilt. A model that assumes "z is up" would already be confused.

#Step 2: Cut windows and remember where each came from

Use the settings from Edge Impulse's own motion tutorial, adapted to 50 Hz: windows of 2 seconds (100 samples) with a stride of 0.5 seconds (25 samples). Each 10-second recording gives (500 − 100) ÷ 25 + 1 = 17 windows.

The new idea in this step is groups: for every window, the number of the recording it came from. You'll need it in Step 4.

#Step 3: Extract features and look at them

Five features per axis, fifteen in all: mean, standard deviation, RMS, the dominant frequency, and how much power sits at that frequency (on a log scale, so big and small motions stay comparable).

Edge Impulse's advice for its feature explorer applies here too: if you can see the classes separate, a model can probably learn to. Idle sits alone in the corner, wave spreads along the bottom, circle sits high on both. Now look closer: each class is made of small, tight clumps. Every clump is one recording, 17 windows that share the same speed, size, and tilt. Keep that picture in mind.

#Step 4: Split by recording, not by window

Those clumps are why a random split would cheat. If 12 windows of a recording go to training and 5 to testing, the test windows are near-copies of training windows, and the score measures memory instead of skill. Instead, hold out whole recordings: the last 3 of each gesture's 10.

The last line is a check worth keeping in every project: the set of recordings that appear on both sides must be empty.

#Step 5: Train three models and weigh them

Accuracy alone can't pick a model for a microcontroller. You also need its size. Here, size means the numbers the model must store to make a prediction:

  • logistic regression: one weight per feature per class, one bias per class, and the scaler's mean and scale for each feature;
  • decision tree: a feature number and a threshold for every split, and a class for every leaf;
  • random forest: all of that, for every tree.

At 4 bytes per number (a float32), that gives a close estimate of the bytes a C version would need.

The forest is no more accurate than logistic regression, yet it's more than 13 times bigger. The tiny tree is smallest of all but makes far more mistakes. On a desktop you'd shrug and pick the forest; on a chip with 256 KB of RAM, shared with everything else the firmware does, logistic regression is the clear choice. That trade-off, accuracy per byte, runs through the rest of this course.

#Step 6: See what it gets wrong

Every mistake is a wave called a circle. That makes physical sense: tilt a side-to-side wave enough and some of its motion lands on the y axis, which is exactly what a circle looks like. The fix isn't a bigger model. It's better data (recordings of waves at more angles) or a feature that doesn't depend on orientation, such as the magnitude of the acceleration. You'll try one in the Practice lesson.

#Step 7: The same pipeline in Edge Impulse

Everything you just wrote by hand has a matching setting in Studio. With your phone connected, record about ten 10-second samples per gesture in Data acquisition (label each one idle, wave, updown, or circle, and vary how you hold the phone). Then:

Studio measures windows in milliseconds, not samples, so a 2000 ms window covers 2 seconds whatever rate your phone records at. That avoids the sample-rate mismatch from the Notes. Studio splits training and test data by sample (each 10-second recording), which matches what you did in Step 4.

#The finished pipeline

Here are all the steps in one cell, without the charts. It runs on its own in a fresh notebook and prints the comparison table.

1Why does Step 2 record a groups entry for every window?

  • The windows are already in time order inside each recording; groups is used for something else.

  • Windows from one recording overlap and share speed, size, and tilt, so splitting them up would leak test data into training.

  • fit never sees groups; it's only used to choose which windows are held out.

Show answer

B. Windows from one recording overlap and share speed, size, and tilt, so splitting them up would leak test data into training.

2Logistic regression and the random forest score within one point of each other. Why pick logistic regression for the device?

  • When accuracy is equal, the smaller and simpler model wins on a device where every kilobyte is shared with the rest of the firmware.

  • Neither model type always wins; here they happen to tie on accuracy.

  • They can (a forest is just many if-statements), but this one costs 13 times the memory for no gain.

Show answer

A. When accuracy is equal, the smaller and simpler model wins on a device where every kilobyte is shared with the rest of the firmware.

3All the mistakes are waves predicted as circles. What would most likely fix them?

  • It has already converged; the problem is that tilted waves really do look like circles in these features.

  • The forest makes similar mistakes; capacity isn't the issue.

  • The confusion comes from tilt moving wave motion onto the y axis, so the data or the features have to account for tilt.

What you'll learn

  • Predict window counts and overlap for any stream, and label windows that cross a change.
  • Spot aliasing and choose a safe sampling rate.
  • Build a feature that doesn't change when a device is rotated.
  • Measure how much a random split inflates accuracy on overlapping windows.
  • Build an anomaly detector trained only on normal data, and a regression model that estimates a number.

Each exercise uses a new situation. Try it in Colab before opening the solution, and run the warm-up cell first, since later cells reuse np.

#Warm-up

A 12-second recording at 50 Hz has 600 samples. With windows of 100 samples and a stride of 50, how many windows are there, and how much does each overlap the next?

#Exercise 1: How stride multiplies your data

Write window_stats(n, size, stride) that returns the number of windows and the overlap. Print a table for one minute of data at 50 Hz (3,000 samples) with 2-second windows (100 samples) and strides of 100, 50, 25, 10, and 1.

Need a hint?

Count = (n − size) // stride + 1, and overlap = 1 − stride / size.

Show solution

Going from stride 25 to stride 1 multiplies the windows by 25, but at 99% overlap each new window differs from the last by a single sample. That's 25 times the training time for very little new information, and 25 times the inferences per second on a device.

#Exercise 2: Drop the windows that can't be labeled

A recording has per-sample labels: 120 samples of walk, then 80 of run, then 100 of walk. Write label_windows(sample_labels, size, stride, min_purity=0.8) that returns the windows to keep as (start, label, purity) and the ones to drop. Use windows of 50 with a stride of 25.

Need a hint?

np.unique(values, return_counts=True) gives each label and how often it appears. Purity is the biggest count divided by the window size.

Show solution

The window at 175 is a perfect 50/50 tie. np.unique sorts labels alphabetically, so argmax picks run only because "r" comes before "w". Keeping a window like that would teach the model a coin toss, which is exactly why the purity threshold exists.

#Exercise 3: The fan that looked slow

A desk fan wobbles 12 times per second. Write dominant_hz(signal_hz, rate) that samples a sine wave of that frequency for 4 seconds at rate and returns the strongest frequency the FFT finds. Try rates of 15, 20, 30, and 50 Hz. Before running, predict what 15 Hz will show.

Need a hint?

np.fft.rfftfreq(number_of_samples, d=1 / rate) gives the frequency of each FFT bin. Below the Nyquist limit, a frequency f sampled at rate r shows up at |f − r|.

Show solution

At 15 and 20 Hz the fan appears to wobble at 3 and 8 Hz, which are |12 − 15| and |12 − 20|. Both rates are below 24 Hz, twice the real frequency. At 30 Hz and above the truth comes through. A model trained on the 15 Hz data would learn that "fan on" means a slow 3 Hz wobble, and nothing about it would look wrong.

#Exercise 4: A feature that ignores tilt

In the Build-along, tilted waves were mistaken for circles because per-axis features change when the device rotates. Build a 2-second wave (0.8 g side to side on x at 1.5 Hz, gravity on z), then rotate it 90° around z so the motion moves onto y. Print the x and y standard deviations and the standard deviation of the magnitude, np.linalg.norm(window, axis=1), for both versions.

Need a hint?

A 90° turn around z is the matrix [[0, -1, 0], [1, 0, 0], [0, 0, 1]]. Apply it to every row with window @ R.T.

Show solution

The x and y features swap completely, so a model that learned "wave means big x_std" fails on the turned device. Rotation never changes a vector's length, so the magnitude's statistics are identical. The trade-off: magnitude throws away direction, so it can't tell a wave from an up-down motion of the same size. Real projects usually keep both kinds of feature.

#Exercise 5: Measure the leak

Generate 30 recordings that alternate between walk and jog (the generator is below). Cut 2-second windows with a 0.5-second stride and compute mean, standard deviation, and dominant frequency per axis. Train a random forest twice: once with train_test_split on windows, once with GroupShuffleSplit on recordings. Compare the accuracies.

Need a hint?

GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, test_size=0.3, random_state=0).split(X, y, groups) yields one pair of index arrays, so wrap it in next(...). Use random_state=0 for both splits and both forests.

Show solution

The random split reports a perfect score because nearly every test window has a twin in training from the same recording, with the same tilt in its mean features. The grouped split asks the real question, "how does it do on a recording it has never seen?", and the answer is much lower. Only the second number predicts what happens when a new person straps on the device.

#Exercise 6: Catch a failing motor without any failures

A motor turns about 30 times a second, and a vibration sensor samples it at 400 Hz. You have plenty of recordings of it running normally, but none of it failing. A worn bearing would add a faint tone near 87 Hz. Build an anomaly detector:

  1. Compute features for 0.5-second windows (200 samples): log power in four frequency bands (0 to 45, 45 to 75, 75 to 120, and 120 to 200 Hz) plus the RMS.
  2. Fit a StandardScaler and KMeans(n_clusters=4) on normal windows only.
  3. Score a window by its distance to the nearest cluster center, and set the threshold at the 99th percentile of the training scores.
  4. Report the false-alarm rate on new normal windows and the share of faulty windows caught. Then try thresholds at the 90th and 95th percentiles.
Need a hint?

kmeans.transform(features) returns the distance from each row to every cluster center, so .min(axis=1) is the distance to the nearest one. Remember to scale with the same StandardScaler you fitted on the training windows.

Show solution

The detector never saw a faulty window, yet it catches most of them, because a fault puts energy into the 75 to 120 Hz band where healthy windows have almost none. The threshold is a dial between two costs: lower it and you catch more of the faint faults, but you also raise false alarms on a healthy motor. Which way to turn it depends on whether a missed fault or a needless inspection costs more. Edge Impulse's Anomaly Detection (K-Means) block works the same way: clusters around normal data, and a score based on distance to the nearest one.

#Challenge: Count steps per minute

A fitness band wants to show walking cadence, in steps per minute: a regression problem. Generate 400 four-second windows of walking (50 Hz, z axis only) with cadences between 80 and 135 steps per minute. Compare two estimators on the last 100 windows, using mean absolute error:

  1. No learning: find the FFT peak between 1.0 and 2.5 Hz and multiply by 60.
  2. Regression: train Ridge on the first 300 windows, using as features the power in each FFT bin from 1.0 to 2.5 Hz, divided by the total power in that range.
Need a hint?

With 200 samples at 50 Hz, FFT bins are 0.25 Hz apart, which is 15 steps per minute. A single peak can only land on one of those bins, but the power in the neighboring bins says which way the true cadence lies.

Show solution

The peak picker can only answer in steps of 15, so its error is stuck at a few steps per minute however clean the signal is. The regression model reads the balance of power between neighboring bins and interpolates between them, cutting the error by more than half. It needs only 8 weights (7 bins plus an intercept), which is a fine trade on a microcontroller.

What you'll learn

  • Explain why raw audio samples make a poor model input, and how frames and the FFT produce a spectrogram.
  • Build a mel filterbank, a log-mel spectrogram, and MFCCs from scratch with NumPy and SciPy.
  • Describe how a keyword spotter listens continuously with keyword, unknown, and noise classes.
  • Quantize float32 numbers to int8 with a scale and zero point, and restore them.
  • Predict the worst-case rounding error, and check accuracy before and after quantizing.

Your keyword model scores 94% on your laptop. It's 420 KB of float32 weights. The board you want to use has 1 MB of flash and 256 KB of RAM, which sounds like plenty, until you remember that the firmware, the audio buffers, and the feature code all need room too. The model has to get smaller, and it has to stay accurate.

There are two levers, and this lesson covers both. Shrink the input: one second of audio is 16,000 numbers, but a good feature representation needs about 1,300. Then shrink the weights: store each one in 1 byte instead of 4.

#One second of audio is 16,000 numbers

Microphones for speech usually sample at 16 kHz: 16,000 readings per second, enough to capture frequencies up to 8 kHz, where most of the information in speech lives. Here's a synthetic "word", a tone that glides upward from 400 Hz to 900 Hz with a harmonic above it, buried in a little background hiss.

Plotted as a waveform, this is a dense scribble. The individual samples say almost nothing on their own; what matters is which frequencies are present and how they change over time. That's what a spectrogram shows.

#Frames and the FFT: a spectrogram

The trick is the windowing you learned in Module 3, at a much smaller scale. Cut the second into short frames of 25 ms (400 samples), starting a new one every 10 ms (160 samples). Over 25 ms, the pitch barely changes, so an FFT of one frame gives a clean snapshot of the frequencies at that moment. Stack the snapshots side by side and you have a spectrogram: time across, frequency up, brightness for energy.

98 frames of 257 frequency bins each. The np.hanning window fades each frame in and out, so the sudden cut at the frame edges doesn't smear energy across every frequency. Apple describes the same structure for "Hey Siri": the audio becomes a sequence of frames, each describing the spectrum of about 0.01 seconds.

#The mel scale: spend detail where ears do

The 257 bins are spaced evenly, 31.25 Hz apart. Human hearing isn't even. You easily hear the difference between 200 Hz and 300 Hz, but 7,200 Hz and 7,300 Hz sound almost the same. The mel scale stretches low frequencies and squashes high ones to match:

mel = 2595 × log₁₀(1 + f ÷ 700)

A mel filterbank is a set of overlapping triangles, evenly spaced in mel, each adding up the energy in its range of bins. Narrow triangles at the bottom keep detail where speech needs it; wide ones at the top save numbers where it doesn't. Taking the log of each filter's energy gives a log-mel spectrogram, which Edge Impulse's MFE block produces.

Near 0 Hz the filters are about 50 Hz apart; near 8 kHz they're about 500 Hz apart. The 1e-10 keeps np.log from hitting zero in silent frames.

#MFCCs: compress the shape of the spectrum

Neighboring mel filters are strongly correlated: if one is loud, the next probably is too. A discrete cosine transform (DCT) across the 40 filters re-expresses each frame as a sum of smooth "shapes", from broad to fine. Keeping only the first 13 coefficients keeps the overall shape of the spectrum and drops fine ripples. These are MFCCs, Mel-Frequency Cepstral Coefficients. Edge Impulse's documentation for its MFCC block notes that 13 coefficients are usually retained.

1,274 numbers instead of 16,000, a 12× cut, and the word is still clearly visible in all three. MFCCs are the classic choice for speech. For non-speech sounds (a dog bark, a machine fault, glass breaking), Edge Impulse recommends its MFE or spectrogram blocks, which keep more detail that speech-tuned MFCCs throw away.

#How keyword spotting uses these features

A keyword spotter, the model behind "Hey Siri" or "OK Google", runs on a 1-second window of MFCCs that slides along the audio stream several times a second. Edge Impulse's keyword-spotting tutorial trains three classes: your keyword, unknown (other words), and noise (background sound), with similar amounts of each. The extra classes matter: a model that only knows "keyword" will call every sound a keyword, because it must pick one of its classes.

Because the window slides, one spoken word appears in several consecutive windows. Real systems average or vote over those predictions before they trigger, which cuts false alarms from a single odd window.

#Quantization: 256 levels instead of 4 billion

Now the weights. A float32 can represent about 4 billion different values. Most models don't need that precision; the weights of a layer usually sit in a narrow range like −1 to +1. Quantization maps that range onto the 256 levels of an int8 (−128 to 127), like replacing a fine ruler with a coarse one.

Two numbers define the mapping:

  • scale: how much real value one integer step is worth, (max − min) ÷ 255;
  • zero point: the integer that represents real 0.0, chosen so that min maps to −128.

quantize: q = clip(round(x ÷ scale) + zero point, −128, 127) restore: x̂ = (q − zero point) × scale

Step through four weights to see each line do its job:

The smallest weight lands on −128 and the largest on 127, as designed. Each restored value is within half a step of the original. Now do it for 2,000 weights:

The largest error equals half a step, exactly as rounding promises, and the memory drops by 4×. The zero point isn't 0 because this range isn't centered: it runs further below zero than above.

#Does the model still work?

Rounding every weight by up to half a step sounds risky. Try it on a trained classifier: quantize its weights, restore them, and compare the predictions.

Every prediction is unchanged. A prediction only flips when an example sits so close to the decision boundary that half-step nudges in the weights push it across, and that's rare. Deep networks round thousands of weights per layer and usually lose a little accuracy, though often very little, which is why int8 is the default for microcontrollers. Edge Impulse's Deployment page lets you pick Quantized (int8) or Unoptimized (float32) and compare their accuracy, latency, RAM, and flash before you build.

#Mistakes that break audio models and int8 models

⚠️ Watch out

One outlier ruins the scale. The scale is set by the minimum and maximum, so a single extreme weight stretches the ruler for everyone:

Most weights now share a few dozen levels. Real quantizers clip the range to ignore rare extremes, or give each output channel its own scale (per-channel quantization).

⚠️ Watch out

Training features that don't match the device's features. If training clips were recorded at 44.1 kHz and the board samples at 16 kHz, or the frame length differs by a few milliseconds, every MFCC shifts and accuracy collapses with no error message. Resample training audio to the device's rate and use the exact same feature settings on both. Edge Impulse avoids this by compiling the same processing block into the device code.

⚠️ Watch out

Calibrating with the wrong data. In full int8 models, the inputs and intermediate values (activations) are quantized too, and their ranges come from a calibration set. Calibrate on audio that looks like real use, including quiet rooms and loud ones, or loud inputs will be clipped at 127.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1One second of 16 kHz audio is cut into 400-sample frames with a 160-sample hop. How many frames are there?

  • That would be 16,000 ÷ 160, which ignores that each frame needs 400 samples to fit.

  • ⌊(16,000 − 400) ÷ 160⌋ + 1 = 97 + 1 = 98, the same window formula as Module 3.

  • 40 is the number of mel filters, which counts frequency bands, not frames.

Show answer

B. ⌊(16,000 − 400) ÷ 160⌋ + 1 = 97 + 1 = 98, the same window formula as Module 3.

2Why are mel filters narrow at low frequencies and wide at high ones?

  • The mel scale follows perceived pitch, so equal mel steps are small in Hz at the bottom and large at the top.

  • Speech actually has more energy at low frequencies; the spacing follows perception, not energy.

  • FFT bins are evenly spaced, 31.25 Hz apart here, at every frequency.

Show answer

A. The mel scale follows perceived pitch, so equal mel steps are small in Hz at the bottom and large at the top.

3Weights range from −0.5 to 1.0. What scale and zero point map them to int8?

  • The range has 256 levels but 255 steps between them, and the zero point must shift −0.5 down to −128.

  • −0.5 ÷ 0.00588 ≈ −85, so −0.5 lands at −85 − 43 = −128 and 1.0 at 170 − 43 = 127.

  • That's symmetric quantization sized for ±1.0, which wastes the levels below −0.5.

Show answer

B. −0.5 ÷ 0.00588 ≈ −85, so −0.5 lands at −85 − 43 = −128 and 1.0 at 170 − 43 = 127.

4You quantize a model and accuracy drops from 94% to 61%. What should you check first?

  • Most models lose little at int8; a drop this large points to a specific bug.

  • Outliers stretch the scale and wrong calibration clips real inputs; both cause large drops.

  • Training length affects the float model too, and that one scored 94%.

Show answer

B. Outliers stretch the scale and wrong calibration clips real inputs; both cause large drops.

Key takeaways

  • Raw audio is 16,000 numbers a second; 25 ms frames, an FFT, mel filters, a log, and a DCT turn one second into about 1,300 MFCC values.
  • A spectrogram shows frequencies over time; log-mel energies (MFE) suit general sounds; MFCCs compress them further for speech.
  • Keyword spotters need keyword, unknown, and noise classes, and they slide a 1-second window along the stream.
  • int8 quantization stores each number in 1 byte using a scale and zero point; each restored value is within half a step of the original.
  • Check accuracy after quantizing, watch for outliers that stretch the range, and calibrate on realistic inputs.

  • Post-training quantization (opens in a new tab), Google AI Edge: how LiteRT (formerly TensorFlow Lite) quantizes real networks, including calibration with a representative dataset.
