What you'll learn

  • Generate a labeled audio dataset with keyword, unknown, and noise classes.
  • Convert every clip to a 13 × 98 MFCC array with your own NumPy feature code.
  • Train a small 1D convolutional network in PyTorch and count its bytes.
  • Quantize each weight tensor to int8 with a scale and zero point, load it back, and compare accuracy.
  • Quantize the inputs with a calibrated range, then push to fewer bits and chart accuracy against size.

Here's the plan: a model that listens to one second of sound and decides whether it heard the keyword up, the keyword down, some unknown other word, or just noise. Then you'll make it four times smaller without retraining, and measure exactly what that costs.

The keywords are synthetic: up is a tone that glides upward, down glides downward. That makes the data free to generate and easy to check by eye. Edge Impulse's own tutorial does the same job with recorded speech, and Step 8 maps every step onto it. Name your notebook m4-l2-keyword-int8.ipynb.

#Step 1: Generate the clips

Every clip gets realistic messiness: a random start time, length, pitch, and loudness, plus background hiss and mains hum at 50 or 60 Hz. The unknown class matters as much as the keywords. Without it, the model would learn "any tone is a keyword", because it must always pick one of its classes. Here, unknown sounds are flat tones and tones that step or bend, so the model has to learn the direction of the glide, not just "something happened".

600 clips × 16,000 samples. That's 9.6 million numbers of raw audio, which is exactly why the next step exists.

#Step 2: Turn every clip into MFCCs

This is the feature pipeline from the Notes, with one speed-up: instead of looping over frames, FRAME_INDEX is a 98 × 400 grid of sample positions, so audio[FRAME_INDEX] pulls out all 98 frames in one NumPy operation. The result is transposed to 13 × 98 (coefficients × time), the shape PyTorch's 1D convolution expects: channels first, then time.

Each clip shrank from 16,000 numbers to 1,274. The event shows up wherever it happened in the second, which is why the model in Step 4 must not care where in time the pattern sits.

#Step 3: Split and normalize

These clips are independent (each was generated separately), so a random split is fair here. With real recordings you'd split by speaker, for the same reason you split by recording in Module 3.

Each MFCC coefficient has its own typical range, so standardize them, one mean and one standard deviation per coefficient. That's 26 numbers the device must also store and apply before running the model.

#Step 4: Train a small 1D CNN

A 1D convolution slides a small filter along the time axis, looking at 5 frames (50 ms) at a time, so it finds a glide wherever it occurs. AdaptiveMaxPool1d(1) then keeps each filter's strongest response across the whole second, which makes the output independent of when the word was said. Edge Impulse's default network for audio is also built from 1D convolutions over the MFCCs, for the same reason.

3,780 parameters, about 15 KB. Your accuracy may differ by an example or two in Colab, since PyTorch's random numbers can vary between machines. This model would already fit on the Nano 33 BLE Sense; the point of the next steps is to see what quantization does to a model you can inspect completely.

#Step 5: Quantize the weights to int8 by hand

For each weight tensor: find its range, compute a scale and zero point, round to int8, then dequantize and put the result back into a copy of the model. Running the copy shows exactly what the int8 numbers can still do. This is called fake quantization, and it's how quantization is usually evaluated before deployment.

Each tensor gets its own scale, so a layer with small weights isn't forced onto the coarse ruler of a layer with big ones. Biases stay in higher precision here; they're only 52 numbers, and real int8 runtimes keep them as 32-bit integers for the same reason. The model is now 3.8 times smaller, and accuracy moves by at most an example.

⚠️ Watch out

Notice .copy() in w = p.numpy().copy(). p.numpy() doesn't copy anything: it gives a NumPy view of the same memory as the PyTorch tensor. Without .copy(), p.copy_(...) overwrites w too, and the "max error" line compares the dequantized weights with themselves and prints 0.00000 for every layer. A check that can't fail isn't a check.

#Step 6: Quantize the inputs too

On a microcontroller running a fully int8 model, the inputs are int8 as well, so the MFCCs have to be squeezed into 256 levels. Their range comes from calibration: measure it on training data, then apply the same scale and zero point to every input the device will ever see.

If a real input falls outside the calibrated range, np.clip pins it at −128 or 127. That's why calibration data should include the loudest and quietest situations the device will meet.

#Step 7: How low can the bits go?

int8 isn't the only choice. Some hardware supports 4-bit weights, and fewer bits mean less memory. Generalize the quantizer to any bit width and sweep.

The curve has the shape you'll see on real models: nearly flat from float32 down through 8 and 6 bits (one test clip of difference), then a slide as the ruler gets too coarse to tell weights apart. This task is easy, so even 2 bits survives better than most real models would; a harder task usually loses more at each step. int8 sits in the sweet spot, which is why it's the standard for microcontrollers.

#Step 8: The same pipeline in Edge Impulse

Edge Impulse does each of these steps for recorded audio. If you work in Edge Impulse, keep the project private, and record only your own voice or people who agreed. Its keyword-spotting tutorial links a ready-made dataset of noise and unknown words, so you only need to record your keyword.

The Deployment page shows estimated accuracy, latency, RAM, and flash for both versions side by side, which is exactly the comparison you just made by hand.

#The finished program

Steps 1 to 6 in one cell, without the charts or the sweep. It prints the float32 and int8 results.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does the dataset include an unknown class of flat and bent tones, not just up, down, and noise?

  • The unknown class teaches the model that "a tone happened" isn't enough; it has to be the right glide.

  • The classes are balanced at 150 each either way; unknown is there for what it teaches.

  • Edge Impulse accepts any number of classes; its tutorial uses keyword, unknown, and noise for the same reason this build does.

Show answer

A. The unknown class teaches the model that "a tone happened" isn't enough; it has to be the right glide.

2Why does Step 5 give each weight tensor its own scale and zero point instead of one for the whole model?

  • It's a design choice, not a library limit.

  • Per-tensor ranges fit the ruler to each layer, so a layer with small weights still uses all 256 levels.

  • Each extra scale and zero point adds 8 bytes, so it's slightly larger; it's done for accuracy.

Show answer

B. Per-tensor ranges fit the ruler to each layer, so a layer with small weights still uses all 256 levels.

3In Step 6, the calibration range comes from the training inputs. What happens on the device if a clip is much louder than anything in training?

  • The scale and zero point are fixed constants in the deployed model.

  • np.clip (and the int8 type itself) can't represent values beyond the range, so they're flattened.

  • The standardized MFCCs here range well beyond ±1; their range depends on the audio.

Show answer

B. np.clip (and the int8 type itself) can't represent values beyond the range, so they're flattened.

Key takeaways

  • A keyword spotter needs keyword, unknown, and noise classes, or every sound becomes a keyword.
  • MFCCs shrink each second from 16,000 numbers to 1,274, and a 1D CNN with global max pooling finds the pattern wherever it occurs in the window.
  • Fake quantization (quantize, dequantize, put back, evaluate) measures what an int8 model can do before you deploy it.
  • Give each tensor its own scale and zero point, keep biases at higher precision, and calibrate input ranges on realistic data.
  • int8 cut this model by about 3.8× with almost no accuracy change; below 4 bits accuracy starts to slide.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Replace the CNN with a plain nn.Linear(1274, 64) network on the flattened MFCCs. Compare its parameter count and accuracy with the CNN's, and think about why position in time hurts it.
  • Quantize each output channel of the conv layers with its own scale (per-channel quantization) and see whether 3-bit accuracy improves.
  • Add a fifth class, a "click" made of a very short burst of noise, and check whether the model still separates all classes.

  • Quantization (opens in a new tab), PyTorch documentation: the library's own tools for the scale and zero-point arithmetic you wrote by hand.

  • Check whether a model fits a flash budget as float32 and as int8.
  • Test a quantizer against PyTorch, tame outliers, and pick symmetric or asymmetric quantization.
  • Compute a layer's output using only integer multiplies and a 32-bit accumulator.

Each exercise is a new situation, not a repeat of the build. Run the warm-up first: later cells reuse its imports.

#Warm-up

Edge Impulse's MFCC block measures frames in seconds. With a 20 ms frame length and a 20 ms frame stride, how many frames fit in one second of 16 kHz audio?

With the stride equal to the frame length, the frames sit edge to edge and never overlap.

#Exercise 1: How settings change the feature size

Write mfcc_shape(sample_rate, seconds, frame_s, stride_s, n_coeffs=13) that returns (frames, coefficients). Print the number of features for these four settings.

Need a hint?

Convert seconds to samples first (int(sample_rate * frame_s)), then use the same window formula as Module 3.

Show solution

The sample rate doesn't change the frame count, because frames are defined in time, not samples. The stride does: halving it doubles the features, the model's input size, and the work the device does every second. Edge Impulse-style settings of 20 ms frames with a 20 ms stride halve the input compared with the 25/10 ms speech default.

#Exercise 2: Read the notes off a spectrogram

A clip plays 440 Hz from 0.2 s to 0.5 s and 660 Hz from 0.6 s to 0.9 s, with quiet hiss elsewhere. Compute a power spectrogram (400-sample frames, 160-sample hop, 512-point FFT), find each frame's strongest frequency, call a frame "quiet" if its peak is under 1% of the loudest frame's, and print every change.

Need a hint?

power.argmax(axis=1) gives the strongest bin in every frame at once, and np.fft.rfftfreq(512, d=1 / SR) converts bins to Hz. Print only when the value differs from the previous frame's.

Show solution

Two details reveal how a spectrogram works. The pitches come out as 437.5 and 656.25 Hz because bins are 31.25 Hz apart, so each tone lands in its nearest bin. And each note appears to start 10 ms early: the frame starting at 0.19 s runs to 0.215 s, so it already contains the beginning of the tone.

#Exercise 3: Where the mel scale spends its detail

Using hz_to_mel and mel_to_hz, work out how many Hz a step of 100 mel covers when it starts at 200 Hz, 1,000 Hz, and 6,000 Hz.

Need a hint?

Convert the starting frequency to mel, add 100, convert back, and subtract the starting frequency.

Show solution

The same perceptual step is more than seven times wider at 6 kHz than at 200 Hz. A mel filterbank with evenly spaced filters therefore spends most of its filters below a couple of kilohertz, where vowels and pitch live.

#Exercise 4: Will it fit in flash?

A board has 1,024 KB of flash, and the firmware (drivers, audio buffers, feature code) already uses 350 KB. For a 3,780-parameter CNN, a 120,000-parameter keyword model, and a 300,000-parameter image model, print the size as float32 and as int8, and whether each fits in what's left.

Need a hint?

float32 is 4 bytes per parameter and int8 is 1. Divide by 1,024 for KB, and compare with 1,024 − 350.

Show solution

The image model only fits after quantization. The keyword model fits either way, but its float32 version would take 70% of the remaining flash, leaving little room for the firmware to grow. Flash is only half the story: the model also needs RAM for its activations while it runs, which Module 5 budgets.

#Exercise 5: Test your quantizer against PyTorch

Your quantize and dequantize should obey two rules: every restored value is within half a step of the original, and the result matches a trusted library. Check both on three very different arrays: uniform in ±0.2, standard normal, and exponential (all positive). PyTorch's torch.fake_quantize_per_tensor_affine(x, scale, zero_point, -128, 127) quantizes and dequantizes in one call.

Need a hint?

Compare with np.allclose(ours, theirs). PyTorch wants the scale as a Python float, so pass float(scale). Allow a tiny tolerance in the half-step check (err <= scale / 2 + 1e-6), because float32 rounding adds error in the last digit.

Show solution

The all-positive array gets a zero point of −128, because its minimum is exactly 0, so real 0.0 sits at the bottom of the int8 range. Matching a library bit for bit is the strongest evidence your arithmetic is right, including the rounding rule: both NumPy and PyTorch round halves to the nearest even integer.

#Exercise 6: One outlier, two ranges

5,000 weights are normal with a standard deviation of 0.1, except three outliers at 2.5, −1.8, and 3.1. Quantize them two ways: with the full min/max range, and with a range clipped to the 0.1st and 99.9th percentiles. For each, print the scale, the mean error on the ordinary weights, and the error on the 3.1 outlier.

Need a hint?

np.percentile(w, [0.1, 99.9]) returns both ends of the clipped range. The outliers are w[:3], so the ordinary weights are w[3:].

Show solution

Clipping makes the ordinary weights almost 8 times more precise, and wrecks the outlier, which gets pinned to the edge of the range. Neither choice is free. Whether clipping helps depends on whether those rare big weights matter to the model's output, which is why quantization tools test several range strategies against real accuracy rather than picking one by rule.

#Exercise 7: Symmetric or asymmetric for ReLU outputs?

Symmetric quantization fixes the zero point at 0 and uses scale = max |x| ÷ 127. It's simpler, since there's no zero point to subtract, but it assumes values on both sides of zero. A ReLU's outputs are never negative. Quantize 5,000 ReLU outputs both ways and compare how many of the 256 levels each uses, and the mean error.

Need a hint?

Make the activations with np.maximum(0, rng.normal(0.5, 1, 5000)). For symmetric, q = np.clip(np.round(x / scale), -128, 127) and the restored value is q * scale.

Show solution

Symmetric quantization can never use the levels from −128 to −1 on data that's never negative, so it has half the resolution and twice the error. That's the usual split in practice: weights (roughly centered on zero) are often quantized symmetrically, and activations (often all positive after ReLU) asymmetrically, with a zero point.

#Challenge: A layer computed with integers only

On a microcontroller an int8 layer never touches floats in its inner loop. Compute y = W @ x for a 4 × 64 weight matrix and a 64-long input using symmetric int8 quantization for both, so the zero points are 0:

  1. Quantize W and x to int8 with their own scales.
  2. Multiply as int32 and sum: these sums are the accumulators.
  3. Convert back with one multiplication by scale_w * scale_x.
  4. Compare with the float result, and work out why the accumulator can't be 16-bit.
Need a hint?

With zero points of 0, W ≈ scale_w × Wq and x ≈ scale_x × xq, so W @ x ≈ scale_w × scale_x × (Wq @ xq). Convert to np.int32 before multiplying, or NumPy will multiply in int8 and overflow.

Show solution

Every multiply and add happened on integers, and one float multiplication at the end recovered values within about 0.02 of the float answer. A single product of two int8 numbers can reach 127 × 127 = 16,129, and 64 of them can reach over a million, far past the 32,767 an int16 can hold. That's why int8 kernels accumulate in int32, and why microcontrollers like the Cortex-M4 have instructions that do two multiplies and add both results into a 32-bit accumulator in a single step.

What you'll learn

  • Say what lives in flash and what lives in RAM while a model runs.
  • Count a layer's parameters and turn them into bytes for float32 and int8.
  • Find the peak activation memory of a chain of layers, the number that decides whether a model fits in RAM.
  • Count multiply-accumulates (MACs) and turn them into a first latency estimate.
  • Check that estimate against the deadline your sensor window sets.

Here is a layer with 320 parameters: a 3×3 convolution that turns a 96×96 grayscale image into 32 feature maps. Quantized to int8, its weights take well under a kilobyte. The Arduino Nano 33 BLE Sense has 1 MB of flash, so the weights fit more than two thousand times over.

The layer still can't run on that board. Its output is 96 × 96 × 32 = 294,912 numbers. At one byte each that's 288 KB, and the board's nRF52840 chip has 256 KB of RAM in total, for everything.

A model on a microcontroller can fail in three separate ways: too big for flash, too big for RAM, or too slow for its deadline. Each limit is counted differently, and a design that does well on one often does badly on another. You'll count all three by hand, then check the counts with PyTorch.

#Flash holds what the model knows; RAM holds what it's working on

A laptop and a microcontroller differ by a factor you can't picture until you write it down:

Typical laptop nRF52840 (Nano 33 BLE Sense)
Processor about 3 GHz, 8 or more cores 64 MHz Arm Cortex-M4 with a floating-point unit, 1 core
Long-term storage 512 GB SSD 1 MB flash
Working memory 16 GB RAM 256 KB RAM

16 GB divided by 256 KB is 65,536. Your laptop has as much working memory as sixty-five thousand of these chips.

Flash keeps its contents with the power off and is slow to write, so firmware treats it as read-only while running. It holds the program, the Edge Impulse SDK, the signal-processing (DSP) code, and the model's weights, stored as constant arrays. RAM is fast to read and write and is wiped when power drops. It holds everything that changes: the sensor window being filled, the DSP features, each layer's outputs (called activations), the call stack, and buffers for Bluetooth and serial.

TensorFlow Lite for Microcontrollers (now called LiteRT for Microcontrollers) asks you to reserve one block of RAM for the model's inputs, outputs, and activations, called the tensor arena, and model setup fails if the block is too small. Edge Impulse sizes that block for you, and it shows estimated RAM, flash, and inference time in the On-device performance panel after training, for the target board you chose on the Dashboard. Those estimates are good, but you'll design better models if you can predict them.

#Parameters: count them, then multiply by bytes

A parameter is one number the model learned. Count them layer by layer:

  • Dense layer: every output connects to every input, plus one bias per output: n_in × n_out + n_out.
  • 2-D convolution: one k×k filter for each pair of input and output channels, plus one bias per output channel: k × k × c_in × c_out + c_out.

The image size is missing from the convolution formula. A filter slides across the image and reuses the same weights at every position, so a 96×96 input and a 960×960 input need the same weights.

The hand counts match PyTorch's numel() totals exactly. Now look at the first row. A dense layer fed a raw 2-second accelerometer window (125 samples × 3 axes = 375 values) has 23 times more parameters than the convolution that reads a whole image. Dense layers on wide inputs are where flash goes.

To turn parameters into bytes, multiply by 4 for float32 or by 1 for int8. That's the 4× saving from quantization you met in the last module. Int8 models usually keep their biases as 32-bit integers, which adds a little, so treat "1 byte per parameter" as a slight underestimate.

#Activations: the RAM that weight counts ignore

While a layer runs, it reads its whole input and writes its whole output, so both have to be in RAM at the same moment. Once the layer finishes, its input is no longer needed and that space can be reused by a later layer. A runtime that plans memory this way needs roughly the largest input-plus-output pair in the model, not the sum of every activation.

Step through the search for that pair. The sizes are each layer's output in KB, starting with the input image:

peak jumps to 297, then to 360, and never moves again. The second layer is the problem: it reads the 288 KB feature map and writes a 72 KB one, and both exist at once.

Those numbers came from a real model. PyTorch can report every layer's input and output size with a forward hook, a function that runs each time a layer produces output. ReLU and Flatten are skipped because microcontroller runtimes apply ReLU in place and treat Flatten as a relabeling, with no new memory.

Flash says yes (about 55 KB of 1 MB) and RAM says no (360 KB of 256 KB). This is the most common way a TinyML model fails, and it's invisible if you only look at model size.

The fix is to shrink the early feature maps, because they're the biggest. Giving the first convolution stride=2 makes it step two pixels at a time, so it outputs 48×48 instead of 96×96. Then the first max-pool isn't needed:

The parameter count is exactly the same, because stride doesn't change the filters. The peak drops to 216 KB, which fits on paper. On a real board it's still tight: the sensor buffer, the stack, and the Bluetooth stack all need RAM too, which is why the next lesson builds a full budget table.

#MACs: counting the work

Nearly all of a neural network's arithmetic is multiply-accumulate: multiply a weight by an input value and add the result to a running sum. Counting MACs is counting work.

  • Dense: each weight is used once, so n_in × n_out MACs.
  • Convolution: each weight is used once at every output position, so h_out × w_out × k × k × c_in × c_out MACs.

Here convolutions flip around. Few parameters, but every one is reused thousands of times. To turn MACs into time, you need a clock speed and a cycles-per-MAC figure. With optimized int8 kernels such as Arm's CMSIS-NN, a Cortex-M4 manages very roughly one MAC every one or two clock cycles. Treat that as a planning number to replace with a measurement later.

The original model needs about 66 million MACs, a second or two per image at 64 MHz. The stride-2 fix that rescued RAM barely changes that, and the per-layer list shows why: it only shrank the first layer's work, and most of the work is in the second convolution (32 channels in, 64 out, at 48×48). Memory and speed are separate problems with separate fixes.

Halving every layer's channels cuts the MACs about 4×, because a convolution's work grows with c_in × c_out. That version lands around 250 to 500 ms. It wouldn't keep up with live video, but a camera trap that checks one photo each time motion wakes it could live with half a second.

#The deadline comes from the sensor window

Every TinyML system has a clock it can't argue with: the sensor. If a gesture detector makes a new prediction every 250 ms, then the DSP and the model together must finish in under 250 ms, every time. If they take longer, new windows arrive before the old ones are done. The device either drops windows (and misses gestures) or falls further behind with each prediction.

The green model is idle most of the time, which you'll be glad of in the power module: idle time is time the chip can sleep. The red model's lag grows by 60 ms with every window, without limit. "Usually fast enough" doesn't count; the worst case has to fit.

⚠️ Watch out

Three counting mistakes that sink a TinyML design

  1. Counting weights and calling it "model size". Flash is only one of three limits. A 55 KB model above needed 360 KB of RAM. Always compute peak activations too.
  2. Mixing float32 and int8 numbers. An Edge Impulse estimate for the int8 model and a PyTorch count of float32 bytes differ by 4×. Write the data type next to every number in your budget.
  3. Timing on your laptop and assuming the board is similar. A laptop core runs at roughly 50 times the clock rate and does more work per cycle. A model that takes 0.5 ms in Colab can take tens or hundreds of milliseconds on a Cortex-M4. Estimate from MACs, then measure on the device.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1A 3×3 convolution with 16 input and 16 output channels runs on a 48×48 input. You switch to a 96×96 input. What happens?

  • The weights don't depend on image size, so the parameter count can't change.

  • The same 3×3×16×16 filters slide over a larger image, and the output has four times as many positions.

  • The weights are reused, but every output position still needs its own slot in RAM.

Show answer

B. The same 3×3×16×16 filters slide over a larger image, and the output has four times as many positions.

2A model's int8 weights take 140 KB and its largest input-plus-output pair is 310 KB. Which limit does it break on an nRF52840 (1 MB flash, 256 KB RAM)?

  • 140 KB of weights is well under 1 MB, even with room for the program.

  • 310 KB of activations alive at once is more than the chip's 256 KB, before the stack and buffers are counted.

  • Weights and activations live in different memories with different limits. Adding them together hides the RAM problem.

Show answer

B. 310 KB of activations alive at once is more than the chip's 256 KB, before the stack and buffers are counted.

3A gesture model needs 12.8 million MACs per prediction. At 64 MHz and 1.5 cycles per MAC, can it make a new prediction every 250 ms?

  • 12.8 million × 1.5 cycles is 19.2 million cycles, and at 64 million cycles per second that's 300 ms, not 50.

  • 19.2 million cycles ÷ 64 million per second = 0.3 s, which is over the 250 ms hop, before any DSP time.

  • The work per prediction comes from MACs; parameter count tells you about flash, not time.

Show answer

B. 19.2 million cycles ÷ 64 million per second = 0.3 s, which is over the 250 ms hop, before any DSP time.

4Which change cuts peak activation memory without changing the number of parameters?

  • That removes parameters, and the last layer's tiny output isn't where the peak is.

  • That changes the parameter count, and late feature maps are already small.

  • The filters are identical, but the first feature map shrinks to a quarter of its size, and that's where the peak was.

Show answer

C. The filters are identical, but the first feature map shrinks to a quarter of its size, and that's where the peak was.

Key takeaways

  • Flash holds code and weights; RAM holds the sensor window, features, activations, stack, and buffers.
  • Parameters: n_in × n_out + n_out for dense layers, k × k × c_in × c_out + c_out for convolutions. Multiply by 1 byte for int8 or 4 for float32.
  • Peak RAM for a chain of layers is roughly the largest input-plus-output pair, and it's usually in the first layers of an image model.
  • MACs measure work. Divide MACs × cycles-per-MAC by the clock rate to estimate latency, then confirm on the device.
  • The sensor window's hop sets a hard deadline for DSP plus inference, and the worst case has to fit.

  • MCUNet: Tiny Deep Learning on IoT Devices (opens in a new tab) is the MIT paper that showed peak activation memory, not weights, is what stops image models from fitting on microcontrollers.

What you'll learn

  • Write a profile() function that reports parameters, peak activations, and MACs for any small PyTorch model.
  • Time a model properly with time.perf_counter: warm up, repeat, and report the median and the worst case.
  • Turn MACs into an on-device latency estimate and check it against a deadline.
  • Build a budget table that counts the firmware around the model, then pick a model with evidence.

Your team is building a wrist-worn gesture remote on an Arduino Nano 33 BLE Sense. It reads the accelerometer at 62.5 Hz, classifies the last 2 seconds of motion as idle, snake, updown, or wave, and sends the gesture name to a phone over Bluetooth. It makes a new prediction every 250 ms, so a wave is noticed within a quarter of a second.

Three teammates each propose a model. One copied a convolutional network from a desktop activity-recognition tutorial. One wrote a small CNN. One wrote a small dense network. All three reach similar accuracy on your test set. Your job is to decide which ones can actually ship, with numbers to back the decision.

By the end you'll have a stacked chart of flash and RAM for each candidate and a pass or fail verdict on every limit. The same notebook works for any model you build later in the course, including your capstone.

#Step 1: Write the device down as numbers

A budget starts with the fixed facts. The window size and sample rate set the input shape (125 samples × 3 axes), the prediction rate sets the deadline, and the board sets the limits.

The Arduino IDE reports 983,040 bytes (960 KB) of program space for this board, because a bootloader keeps the rest of the 1 MB. The RAM is the full 256 KB.

375 values per window is the same frame size that appears in Edge Impulse's example output for these four gestures, so these are realistic numbers.

#Step 2: The three candidates

Each model takes a tensor shaped (batch, axes, samples) and returns four scores.

All three produce one row of four scores, so they're drop-in replacements for each other. That's what makes a fair comparison possible.

#Step 3: Profile parameters, peak activations, and MACs

This is the counting from the notes, wrapped in one function. A forward hook records each layer's input and output sizes and adds up MACs for Conv1d and Linear layers. For a 1-D convolution, each weight is used once per output position, so the MACs are output_length × kernel × c_in × c_out.

Read across the rows. The desktop CNN has about 35 times the parameters of the small CNN and over 130 times the MACs. Its third convolution alone has 128 × 128 × 9 weights, because convolution parameters grow with input channels times output channels. The small dense network has the fewest MACs by far: a dense layer uses each weight exactly once.

In float32 the desktop CNN's weights take about 874 KB. That's 91% of the program space before a single line of firmware.

#Step 4: Time each model on your laptop, the careful way

time.perf_counter() is Python's high-resolution clock for measuring short intervals. The careful recipe has three parts. Run a few warm-up calls first, because the first call pays one-time costs such as memory allocation. Time many calls, because any single run can be delayed by something else on the machine. Report the median for typical speed and a high percentile for the bad cases.

On a laptop every candidate finishes in well under a millisecond, and the first call is the slowest, which is why it's thrown away. Now compare the medians with the MAC counts. The MAC ratios between models are far bigger than the time ratios. For tiny models, a laptop spends most of each call on PyTorch's own overhead, not arithmetic, so laptop timing can't rank them the way a microcontroller would.

⚠️ Watch out

Timing mistakes that give you a meaningless number

  • Timing one call. You get the warm-up cost, or a moment when the operating system was busy. Always repeat and take the median.
  • Using time.time(). It follows the wall clock, which can be adjusted while your code runs, and on some systems it ticks too coarsely for microsecond work. Use time.perf_counter() for intervals.
  • Forgetting torch.no_grad(). Without it PyTorch records extra information for training, so you time work the device will never do.

#Step 5: Estimate the time on the microcontroller

To predict the board, go back to MACs. Using the planning figure of one to two cycles per int8 MAC on a 64 MHz Cortex-M4, the estimate is MACs × cycles ÷ clock. The raw-data feature block does almost no work, but we'll reserve 5 ms for reading the window and scaling it. The team's rule: DSP plus inference may use at most half the 250 ms hop, leaving the rest for Bluetooth and for sleeping.

The desktop CNN needs roughly 360 to 730 ms per prediction, three to six times the 125 ms limit, so it fails even in int8. The other two need about 5 to 11 ms, most of it the DSP allowance. The ratio column is the warning from the notes in numbers: for the model alone, the board is somewhere between tens and thousands of times slower than the laptop, and the factor changes from model to model.

#Step 6: Count the whole firmware, then decide

The model is only one line of the budget. The Arduino core and Mbed OS, the Bluetooth library, the Edge Impulse SDK, the stack, and the sensor buffers all need room. The fixed numbers below are rough figures for this board; replace them with your own. When you compile, the Arduino IDE prints lines like "Sketch uses … bytes of program storage space" and "Global variables use … bytes of dynamic memory", and those are the numbers to use.

The pass rule keeps 20% of flash and RAM free, because every real project grows: a bug fix, a logging feature, a bigger Bluetooth buffer. Read the verdicts:

  • Desktop CNN, float32 fails flash outright. Desktop CNN, int8 fits in memory but fails the deadline, as Step 5 showed.
  • Small CNN and small dense pass everything in both data types, with lots of room.

Notice where the RAM goes. For these gesture models, the operating system and Bluetooth use far more RAM than the model. That's normal for motion sensing. Image and audio models are where activations take over, as you'll see in the practice exercises.

With two models passing, budget isn't the tiebreaker anymore. Pick by accuracy on real-world data (next module) and by energy: the small dense network does about 14 times fewer MACs than the small CNN, so the chip can sleep longer between predictions.

#The finished notebook

Put the steps together into one file you can reuse. Change candidates and the constants, and run it again for any device.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does the notebook throw away the warm-up calls before computing the median?

  • It's the other way around: the first calls are usually the slowest.

  • Memory allocation and setup happen once. Including them would make typical latency look worse than it is.

  • The clock is fine; it's the model call that's slower at first.

Show answer

B. Memory allocation and setup happen once. Including them would make typical latency look worse than it is.

2The desktop CNN in int8 uses about 59% of flash and well under 256 KB of RAM. Why does it still fail?

  • Int8 is the format microcontroller runtimes are best at.

  • It fits in memory, but at one to two cycles per MAC on a 64 MHz chip, it can't keep up with a prediction every 250 ms.

  • Parameters live in flash. RAM holds activations, and this model's are small.

Show answer

B. It fits in memory, but at one to two cycles per MAC on a 64 MHz chip, it can't keep up with a prediction every 250 ms.

3The small CNN and small dense both pass. Why would you lean toward the dense network if accuracy is equal?

  • Fewer operations means less active time per prediction. Module 7 turns that into days of battery life.

  • It actually has about twice the parameters of the small CNN; both are tiny compared with the firmware.

  • Neither is always better; that's why you test both on real data.

Show answer

A. Fewer operations means less active time per prediction. Module 7 turns that into days of battery life.

Key takeaways

  • Write the device spec as constants first: input shape, deadline, flash, RAM, and clock.
  • One profile() function with forward hooks gives parameters, peak activations, and MACs for any sequential model.
  • Time with time.perf_counter(): warm up, repeat, report the median and a high percentile.
  • Laptop timings can't predict microcontroller timings, even in relative terms, for tiny models. Estimate from MACs and confirm on the board.
  • Count the firmware around the model and keep about 20% headroom. For motion models, the OS and Bluetooth usually outweigh the model.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Replace the fixed numbers with the "Sketch uses" and "Global variables use" lines from compiling an empty sketch with the Bluetooth library on your board.
  • Train the small dense network on Edge Impulse and compare its On-device performance estimate with your profile() numbers.

  • Edge Impulse: Deployment (opens in a new tab) shows the int8 and float32 model versions, the EON Compiler, and the resource estimates for your chosen target.

What you'll learn

  • Count parameters, bytes, and MACs for a small audio CNN without help from a framework.
  • Find peak activation memory with the pair rule, and see where the rule breaks.
  • Measure latency correctly with time.perf_counter.
  • Sweep a design choice (input resolution) and find the largest value that fits every limit.

The build-along used motion data, where the firmware outweighed the model. These exercises move to audio and images, where the model starts to fight for memory. Every solution is plain Python or NumPy, so each one runs on its own.

#Warm-up

Answer these in your head or on paper, then check:

  1. How many parameters does a dense layer from 64 inputs to 10 outputs have?
  2. How many bytes is that in float32?
  3. How many parameters does a 5×5 convolution from 3 channels to 8 channels have?
Show solution
  1. 64 × 10 weights + 10 biases = 650.
  2. 650 × 4 bytes = 2,600 bytes, about 2.5 KB.
  3. 5 × 5 × 3 × 8 weights + 8 biases = 608. The image size doesn't matter.

#Exercise 1: Count a keyword spotter's parameters

A keyword spotter turns one second of audio into a 49 × 40 grid of filterbank energies (49 time frames, 40 frequency bands) and treats it like a one-channel image. The model:

Layer Details
Conv2d 3×3, 1 → 8 channels, padding keeps 49×40
MaxPool 2×2, halves height and width (rounding down)
Conv2d 3×3, 8 → 16 channels, padding keeps the size
MaxPool 2×2
Dense flatten, then 3 outputs ("yes", "no", background)

Write a short program that walks these layers, tracks the shape, and prints the total parameters and the int8 and float32 sizes in KB.

Need a hint?

Keep three variables, h, w, and c, and update them as you go. A pool layer changes h and w with //2. The dense layer's input count is h * w * c at that point.

Show solution

The dense layer has 5,763 of the 7,011 parameters, because it connects all 1,920 flattened values to each output. That's typical: in small CNNs the last dense layer often holds most of the weights.

#Exercise 2: Find its peak activation memory

Using the same model, list the size of every tensor (input, then each layer's output) and apply the pair rule: peak = the largest input-plus-output of any layer. Report it for int8 and float32.

Need a hint?

The first convolution's output is 49 × 40 × 8. Then use zip(sizes, sizes[1:]) to walk through neighboring pairs.

Show solution

The peak is the first pooling layer, reading 15,680 values and writing 3,840. Even in float32 this model fits easily in 256 KB, which is one reason keyword spotting was one of the first TinyML successes.

#Exercise 3: Will it keep up?

The device classifies a 1-second window every 250 ms. Turning audio into the 49 × 40 grid takes 35 ms on the board. Count the MACs for each layer (convolution: h_out × w_out × k × k × c_in × c_out; dense: n_in × n_out), then estimate total latency at 64 MHz for 1 and 2 cycles per MAC. Does it fit in half the hop (125 ms)?

Need a hint?

Pool layers do comparisons, not MACs, so leave them out. The second convolution runs on the pooled 24 × 20 grid.

Show solution

The model itself takes only 11 to 22 ms; the DSP is the bigger cost. For audio, always budget the feature extraction too. Edge Impulse reports DSP and classification time separately for this reason.

#Exercise 4: Fix the timing harness

A teammate timed a tiny NumPy network like this and reported "0.03 ms" in the team chat. Run it a few times and you'll see the number jump around.

Rewrite it so it uses time.perf_counter(), does 50 warm-up calls, times 2,000 calls, and prints the first call, the median, and the 99th percentile in microseconds.

Need a hint?

Store each duration in a list. Sort the list, then index at int(0.99 * len(times)) for the 99th percentile. statistics.median gives the median.

Show solution

The median is stable from run to run; the single time.time() reading wasn't. The 99th percentile shows the occasional slow call, which on a real device is the one that misses a deadline. Your numbers will differ from the ones shown here, and none of them say much about a 64 MHz chip.

#Exercise 5: Find the largest camera image that fits

A wildlife camera uses this CNN on a square grayscale image of side r:

  • Conv 3×3, 1 → 16, same size, then 2×2 max-pool
  • Conv 3×3, 16 → 32, same size, then 2×2 max-pool
  • Conv 3×3, 32 → 32, same size, then global average and a 2-way dense layer

After the firmware, sensor buffers, and Bluetooth, 120 KB of RAM is left for activations, and one photo may take up to 1,000 ms (2 cycles per MAC, 64 MHz). Try r in 64, 80, 96, 112, 128, and 160. Plot int8 peak activation and latency against r, with the limits as dashed lines, and print the largest r that meets both.

Need a hint?

Write a function costs(r) that returns (peak_kb, latency_ms). The tensors are: r*r, 16*r*r, 16*(r//2)**2, 32*(r//2)**2, 32*(r//4)**2, 32*(r//4)**2. The MACs come from the three convolutions only.

Show solution

Memory grows with r², and so does time, but the RAM limit is much tighter: only 64×64 fits, while time would allow up to 128×128. The first pool layer, holding the full-resolution 16-channel map and its pooled copy, sets the peak. A stride-2 first convolution would let 96×96 fit, as in the notes.

#Exercise 6: When the pair rule underestimates

The pair rule assumes each tensor is used once, by the next layer. A skip connection breaks that: an early tensor is kept so it can be added back later. In this block, t1 is needed again at the Add step.

Each tensor is created at one step and last read at a later step. A tensor is in RAM at step s if it was created at or before s and is still needed at or after s. Write peak_live(tensors) that returns the largest total at any step, and compare it with the pair rule.

Need a hint?

Store each tensor as (name, size_kb, created_step, last_used_step). The input is created at step 0, and the final output is last used at the last step. For each step from 1 to 5, add up the sizes of tensors that are alive.

Show solution

Holding t1 across three layers adds 36 KB to the peak, half again what the pair rule predicts. That's why MobileNet-style models with skip connections need careful memory planning on microcontrollers, and why Edge Impulse and TensorFlow Lite Micro compute the arena from the real graph instead of a rule of thumb.

#Challenge: Fit a person detector

Design a CNN for 96×96 grayscale images that answers "person or no person" within these limits on the nRF52840:

  • int8 weights at most 250 KB
  • int8 peak activations at most 100 KB
  • at most 800 ms per image (2 cycles per MAC at 64 MHz)
  • at least four convolution layers, so it has a chance of being accurate

Write the model in PyTorch, measure it with the profile() function from the build-along (adapted for Conv2d), and write three sentences explaining which choice saved the most RAM and which saved the most time. There's no single right answer; compare yours with a classmate's.

Need a hint?

Use stride 2 in the first convolution to shrink the big early feature maps. Then look at which layer has the most MACs and try fewer channels there, or a stride-2 convolution in place of a pool.

What you'll learn

  • Choose between Edge Impulse's Arduino library, pre-built firmware, and C++ library, and say what each one contains.
  • Read the core of an Edge Impulse Arduino sketch: signal_t, run_classifier(), and the result struct.
  • Run a parity check that proves the board computes the same scores as Studio.
  • Explain data drift and show it with a lab-versus-field confusion matrix.
  • Order your tests from Studio to the field, and say which bugs each one catches.

Model testing in Edge Impulse says 98%. You flash the board, strap it to your wrist, and wave. The Serial Monitor says snake. You wave again: idle. Up and down: snake.

Nothing about the model changed between the test page and your wrist. What changed was the data. In the lab you held the board flat, the way you held it while recording training samples. On a wrist it sits tilted, so gravity and motion show up on different axes. The model was never shown that, and it fails in a specific, predictable pattern you can read off a confusion matrix.

This lesson covers both halves of the problem: getting the model onto the board correctly, and measuring how good it is once it's there.

#What Edge Impulse builds when you click Build

The Deployment page in Edge Impulse Studio has a search box ("Search deployment options") and a long list of targets. Options that don't support your project's sensor type are greyed out and labeled "Not supported". Three matter for this course's boards:

Option What you download When to use it
Arduino library A .zip with your impulse (DSP code, model, and SDK) as an Arduino library, plus example sketches You want to write your own sketch around the model, for example to light an LED or send Bluetooth messages
Pre-built firmware (shown under your board's name) A ready-to-flash binary for a fully supported board such as the Nano 33 BLE Sense You want to see the model running in minutes, with no code
C++ library The same impulse as plain C++ source Your board isn't an Arduino, or you use another build system

Below the list, Model optimizations lets you pick Quantized (int8) or Unoptimized (float32), and the TFLite or EON Compiler runtime. Studio estimates latency, RAM, and flash for each choice before you build, so you can check them against the budget from the last module.

For the Arduino library, install the .zip with Sketch › Include Library › Add .ZIP Library…, then open File › Examples › your project name_inferencing. On a Nano 33 BLE Sense there are examples for the accelerometer, microphone, and camera. Rev2 boards have their own nano_ble33_sense_rev2 versions of the motion examples, because the Rev2 uses a different motion sensor.

For pre-built firmware, the downloaded .zip contains flash scripts (flash_windows.bat, flash_mac.command, flash_linux.sh). After flashing, edge-impulse-run-impulse prints predictions in your terminal; add --continuous to classify without pauses on boards that support it.

#One function call does the work

Here is the heart of Edge Impulse's accelerometer example for the Nano 33 BLE Sense. It fills a buffer at the sampling interval the model was trained on, wraps the buffer in a signal_t, and calls run_classifier():

Every name in capitals comes from the generated library: EI_CLASSIFIER_DSP_INPUT_FRAME_SIZE is 375 for a 2-second, 3-axis window at 62.5 Hz, and EI_CLASSIFIER_INTERVAL_MS is the gap between samples (16 ms). Two lines decide whether the board sees the same kind of data as training: the unit conversion, and the wait that keeps the sample rate right. Get either wrong and the model receives numbers it has never seen. The result also carries result.timing.dsp and result.timing.classification in milliseconds, which are your real latency measurements.

#Test 1 on the board: does it agree with Studio?

Before testing accuracy, prove the deployment is correct. The Arduino library includes a static_buffer example for exactly this. In Studio, open Live classification, load a test sample, click a row under the detailed result, and use Copy to clipboard next to Raw features. Paste those numbers into the features[] array in the sketch, upload it, and open the Serial Monitor at 115,200 baud.

The board should print scores that match what Studio showed for the same window, to within small rounding differences. If they don't, the problem is in the build, not the data: a float32 model tested in Studio but an int8 model deployed, a stale library still installed from an older build, or a sketch from a different project. This check takes ten minutes and rules out a whole class of bugs before you spend an afternoon field testing.

#Why the lab score doesn't travel: data drift

Data drift means the data a deployed model sees differs from the data it was trained and tested on. For TinyML the usual causes are physical: sensor placement and orientation, a different sample rate, a different user, background noise, lighting, temperature, or a new board revision with a different sensor.

To see it happen, here's a small simulation of the gesture remote. Each 2-second window gets nine features (per axis: the average, the strength of the motion, and the dominant frequency), and a small neural network learns the four classes. The training and test data come from the lab, with the board held roughly flat.

The lab test set is held out from training, so this is an honest lab number. Now keep the model fixed and change one thing: how far the board is tilted when it's worn.

The model handles small tilts, because the training data had a little wobble in it. Past about 20 degrees, accuracy falls off a cliff. A wrist is easily 40 degrees off flat. Note what didn't happen: no error message, no crash, no warning. The model returns confident-looking scores the whole time.

#Read the confusion matrix, not the headline number

An accuracy of 62% could mean every class is a bit worse, or one class is perfect and another is never recognized. A confusion matrix tells you which. Each row is the true class, each column is what the model predicted, and the diagonal holds the correct answers. Edge Impulse's Model testing page uses the same layout.

Recall for a class is the share of its real windows the model got right: the diagonal cell divided by its row total. In the field, idle and snake survive while updown and wave collapse, with snake the most common wrong answer. That pattern has a physical explanation: tilting the board mixes the x and z axes, so a wave and an up-down motion both show up on two axes at once, which is what snake looks like in the training data.

The matrix also points at the fix. You don't need a bigger model; you need training data recorded the way the device is worn:

Same network, same number of training windows, much better field accuracy. Collecting data where and how the device will be used is the single most effective fix for drift.

#A test ladder from Studio to the field

Each kind of test catches different mistakes, so run them in order and don't skip rungs:

Rung Where Catches
1. Model testing Studio, on held-out test data Overfitting, weak classes, bad labels
2. Parity check Board, with static_buffer Build mistakes: wrong model version, stale library, int8 versus float32 surprises
3. Bench test Board, live sensor, at your desk Wrong units, wrong sample rate, sensor wiring, latency
4. Field test Board, real placement, real users and places Data drift: placement, people, noise, lighting, weather

Only rung 4 measures what you care about. The others make sure that when rung 4 goes badly, you know the cause is the data and not a bug.

⚠️ Watch out

Three ways to fool yourself after deployment

  1. Reusing the Studio score as the device's accuracy. It measures rung 1 only. Report field accuracy separately, with the conditions you tested.
  2. Testing one model version and deploying another. Model testing lets you test Unoptimized (float32) or Quantized (int8). Test the one you're going to ship.
  3. Changing how the sketch samples. Reading the sensor as fast as the loop runs, or forgetting the g to m/s² conversion, gives the model data at a different rate or scale from training. Keep the example's sampling loop.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1The board's scores for a pasted static_buffer sample differ completely from Studio's for the same sample. What's the most likely cause?

  • The parity check uses the exact same numbers as Studio, so drift can't be the cause.

  • Same input and different output means the code on the board isn't the impulse you tested.

  • A wrong baud rate gives garbled text, not believable but different scores.

Show answer

B. Same input and different output means the code on the board isn't the impulse you tested.

2In a field confusion matrix, the "wave" row reads 8 correct out of 30, with most of the rest in the "snake" column. What does that tell you?

  • The row is the true class: 8 of 30 right, and the off-diagonal cells say where the rest went.

  • Snake's recall is read from the snake row, not from the snake column.

  • Overall accuracy needs every row; one row gives one class's recall.

Show answer

A. The row is the true class: 8 of 30 right, and the off-diagonal cells say where the rest went.

3Your model scores 98% in the lab and 64% on a wrist. Which change is most likely to help?

  • The model already separates lab data well; more capacity doesn't teach it about wrist placement.

  • Quantization costs at most a point or two here; it didn't cause a 34-point drop.

  • The drop comes from data the model never saw. Showing it that data is the direct fix.

Show answer

C. The drop comes from data the model never saw. Showing it that data is the direct fix.

Key takeaways

  • The Arduino library gives you code to build on; pre-built firmware gives a quick demo with edge-impulse-run-impulse; the C++ library works with any toolchain.
  • run_classifier() takes a signal_t and fills an ei_impulse_result_t with labels, scores, and DSP and classification times.
  • Run a static_buffer parity check first: same input, same output, or the build is wrong.
  • Data drift is a change between training and deployment data, and for TinyML it's usually physical: placement, rate, users, environment.
  • Read per-class recall from a confusion matrix; the pattern of mistakes usually points to the cause and the fix.

#Further reading

  • Edge Impulse: Deployment (opens in a new tab) lists every deployment target and the int8, float32, and EON Compiler options.
  • Edge Impulse: Running your impulse on Arduino (opens in a new tab) walks through installing the library and the static_buffer parity check step by step.
  • Edge Impulse: Model testing (opens in a new tab) explains the test set, per-class accuracy, and how to test the int8 version.

m6-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Extend Edge Impulse's accelerometer example so each prediction is logged as a CSV line with the true label.
  • Clean a field log by dropping the windows that straddle a change of gesture.
  • Compute a confusion matrix, per-class recall and precision, and accuracy per tester.
  • Put an honest uncertainty range on field accuracy by resampling whole blocks, not single windows.
  • Check on-device latency from the timings the board reports.

Studio's Model testing page can't tell you how the gesture remote performs on three different people, worn on a wrist, in a hallway. A field test can, but only if every prediction is written down next to what the person was really doing. That pairing is the whole job of this build.

Here's the finished output: a report you can paste into a design doc.

#Step 1: Log every prediction with the truth next to it

Start from the nano_ble33_sense_accelerometer example in your project's Arduino library (on a Rev2 board, the nano_ble33_sense_rev2 version). Keep its sampling loop exactly as it is, since that loop sets the units and sample rate. Add two things: a way for a partner to mark which gesture the tester is doing, and one CSV line per prediction.

Upload it, open the Serial Monitor at 115,200 baud, and have your partner type a letter in the message box and press Enter each time the tester switches gesture. The output looks like this:

The block number goes up with every key press, even if the gesture is the same as before. That matters in Step 3. Save each tester's lines as a file (field_A.csv, field_B.csv, …), by copying from the Serial Monitor or by using a serial terminal program that logs to a file.

📝 Note

This simple loop records a window, then classifies it, so it ignores motion during the few milliseconds of classification. For a field test that's fine. For the product, the nano_ble33_sense_accelerometer_continuous example records and classifies at the same time.

#Step 2: Load the logs

So the notebook runs before you have hardware, the next cell writes three logs in exactly the sketch's format. Tester A held the board flat, as in training; testers B and C wore it on the wrist. The predictions are simulated from a realistic error pattern; replace these files with your own and every later cell works unchanged.

Each row is one 2-second window. Lines arrive about 2,015 ms apart: 2,000 ms of sampling plus DSP, classification, and printing.

#Step 3: Drop the windows that straddle a change

When your partner presses a key, the tester hasn't started the new gesture yet. The first window of every block is mostly reaction time and the end of the old gesture. Scoring it would blame the model for a human delay, so drop the first prediction of each block. This is why the sketch counts blocks rather than relying on the label: two blocks in a row can have the same gesture.

Cleaning raises accuracy by several points, and it's the honest number: it measures the model on windows that contain one gesture.

#Step 4: Confusion matrix and per-class scores

Overall accuracy hides which gestures fail. Build the matrix and compute two scores per class: recall (of the real waves, how many were called wave) and precision (of the windows called wave, how many really were).

Wave and updown are the weak classes, with the lowest recall. Snake has the lowest precision, because it collects many of the mistakes: when the model is unsure about a tilted up-down, it says snake. A user would experience this as "the remote keeps doing the snake action when I move it up and down".

#Step 5: Accuracy for each tester

Now split by tester. If the problem is placement, it should show up as a difference between the flat and wrist sessions.

Tester A, holding the board the way training data was recorded, gets lab-like accuracy. Both wrist testers are far lower. One field number for "the model" would have averaged these together and hidden the cause.

#Step 6: How sure are you about that number?

A field test is a sample, and the accuracy you measured would come out a bit different if you ran it again. A bootstrap estimates how much: resample your data with replacement thousands of times and see how much the accuracy moves.

There's a trap. Windows from the same block are not independent: same person, same minute, same way of wearing the board. Resampling single windows pretends you have hundreds of independent trials and gives a falsely narrow range. Resample whole blocks instead.

The block-based range is wider. With 24 blocks you know field accuracy to within several percentage points, not to one decimal place. To narrow it, add more blocks: more testers, more sessions, more places. More windows from the same block barely help.

#Step 7: Latency, measured on the board

The log also carries the board's own timings. They replace the estimates from the budget module with measurements.

For this motion model, DSP takes far longer than the neural network, and the whole thing uses a small slice of the budget.

#The finished report

Put it together as one script you run after every field session. It reads all field_*.csv files in the folder and prints a summary with pass or fail against the targets you set before testing.

The verdict names the next action. That's the point of writing targets down before the test: the report tells you what to do, not just how you did.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does the sketch print a block number instead of relying on changes in the truth column?

  • Space isn't the issue; the two columns are about the same size.

  • If round 1 ends with wave and round 2 starts with wave, the truth never changes, but the tester still paused.

  • It sends them fine; the block counter is about cleaning the log afterwards.

Show answer

B. If round 1 ends with wave and round 2 starts with wave, the truth never changes, but the tester still paused.

2Resampling windows gives a 95% range of 77% to 86%. Resampling blocks gives 75% to 88%. Which should go in the report?

  • Narrower only because it treats correlated windows as independent trials, which they aren't.

  • Blocks are closer to independent trials, so their spread is the honest uncertainty.

  • A single number without a range invites people to read differences that are just noise.

Show answer

B. Blocks are closer to independent trials, so their spread is the honest uncertainty.

3Updown has recall 74% and snake has precision 71%. What does a user notice?

  • Low updown recall means up-downs are missed; low snake precision means many "snake" outputs weren't snakes.

  • Snake recall is high; precision is what's low.

  • Users experience individual classes, not the average.

Show answer

A. Low updown recall means up-downs are missed; low snake precision means many "snake" outputs weren't snakes.

Key takeaways

  • Log the truth on the device, next to each prediction, so field results can be scored without guesswork.
  • Drop windows that straddle a change; they measure human reaction time, not the model.
  • Report per-class recall and precision, and split by tester or condition to find the cause.
  • Bootstrap over blocks, not windows, to get an honest uncertainty range.
  • Write pass targets before testing so the report tells you what to do next.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Add a column for result.classification scores of all four classes, and plot how often the right class was second.
  • Have the sketch flash the built-in LED when it predicts wave, so the tester sees mistakes live.
  • Add a fourth tester in a noisy place, such as walking down a corridor, and see whether idle survives.

#Further reading

  • Edge Impulse: Live classification (opens in a new tab) shows how to record new samples from the device and move misclassified ones into your training set.
  • scikit-learn: confusion_matrix (opens in a new tab) documents the function and the row and column convention.

m6-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Compute per-class recall, precision, and balanced accuracy from a confusion matrix.
  • Decide whether a board passes a parity check against Studio, including near-ties.
  • Find which input features drifted between lab and field, and connect them to a physical cause.
  • Show what a sample-rate mistake does to a frequency feature.
  • Estimate how many field-test blocks you need for a given precision.

These exercises use small arrays you can check by hand, so you can focus on the reasoning. Every solution runs on its own.

#Warm-up

A person detector was tested on 200 camera frames. It found 45 of the 50 frames with a person and raised 10 false alarms on the 150 empty frames. Work out accuracy, recall for "person", and precision for "person".

Show solution
  • True positives 45, false negatives 5, false positives 10, true negatives 140.
  • Accuracy = (45 + 140) / 200 = 92.5%.
  • Recall = 45 / 50 = 90%: of the real people, how many it found.
  • Precision = 45 / (45 + 10) = 81.8%: of its "person" alerts, how many were right.

#Exercise 1: Which keyword needs more data?

Here is a keyword spotter's confusion matrix from a field test (rows are the truth, columns the prediction):

Write a program that prints recall and precision for each class and the overall accuracy. Then answer: which class should you collect more training data for, and what should those recordings sound like?

Need a hint?

Recall divides the diagonal by the row total; precision divides it by the column total. With NumPy, cm[i, :].sum() is row i and cm[:, i].sum() is column i.

Show solution

"no" has the worst recall, and 18 of its 29 misses went to "unknown". The model doesn't recognize many real "no"s as the keyword. Collect more "no" recordings from the voices, distances, and rooms where the field test happened. The low precision of "unknown" is the same problem seen from the other side: it's absorbing those missed "no"s.

#Exercise 2: The 96.5% fall detector

A fall detector was tested on 1,000 windows: 950 normal activity and 50 real falls. It caught 20 falls and raised 5 false alarms. Compute accuracy, fall recall, and balanced accuracy (the average of the recall of each class). Then compute the accuracy of a "model" that always says "no fall".

Need a hint?

Normal-class recall is the true negatives divided by 950. Balanced accuracy for two classes is (recall_fall + recall_normal) / 2.

Show solution

The detector misses 60% of falls and still scores 96.5%, barely above the 95% you'd get by never detecting anything. When one class is rare, report its recall and the balanced accuracy, never accuracy alone.

#Exercise 3: Does the board agree with Studio?

You ran the static_buffer example on five test samples. Here are the scores Studio showed (float32) and the scores the board printed (int8 model), for classes idle, snake, updown, and wave:

Write a check that passes if every score is within 0.05 of Studio's, and the top label matches whenever Studio's top score beats its second by at least 0.10. Print a line per sample.

Need a hint?

For each sample, max(abs(a - b) for a, b in zip(s, b)) gives the largest difference. Sort Studio's scores to find the margin between first and second place.

Show solution

Sample 4 flips from snake to updown, but Studio itself only preferred snake by 0.04. Rounding to int8 can tip a near-tie either way, so that's expected. A flip on a sample with a large margin, or any difference above about 0.05, would point to a build problem.

#Exercise 4: Which feature drifted?

The gesture model uses nine features: the mean, motion strength (RMS), and dominant frequency on each axis. The next cell makes 200 lab windows and 200 field windows of features. For each feature, compute the standardized shift: (field mean − lab mean) / lab standard deviation. Plot the shifts as bars, mark ±1 with dashed lines, and print the features beyond it. What physical change explains them?

Need a hint?

lab.mean(axis=0) and lab.std(axis=0) give one value per feature column. A shift of 1 means the field average moved by one lab standard deviation.

Show solution

Gravity moved from z toward x, which is exactly what tilting the board by about 40 degrees does. You can find this without labels: comparing feature averages needs only the raw field data. That makes it a cheap early warning to run on any new deployment before anyone has labeled anything.

#Exercise 5: The sample-rate bug

A teammate "simplified" the sketch by deleting the wait in the sampling loop. The board now fills its 125-sample buffer at about 125 Hz instead of 62.5 Hz, but the DSP block still assumes 62.5 Hz. A tester waves at 2 Hz. Generate both versions of the window and print the dominant frequency the model's features would report.

Need a hint?

Build the time axis from the real sample rate: t = np.arange(125) / real_hz. Compute the frequency axis from the rate the model assumes: np.fft.rfftfreq(125, 1 / 62.5).

Show solution

Sampling twice as fast squeezes 2 seconds of the model's expectations into 1 second of real motion, so every movement looks half as fast. No error appears anywhere. This is why the Edge Impulse examples wait EI_CLASSIFIER_INTERVAL_MS between samples, and why your bench test should check the time between log lines.

#Exercise 6: How many blocks do you need?

Each field block has its own accuracy, because people and places differ. Simulate field tests where each block's accuracy is drawn from rng.beta(8.5, 1.5) (average 85%) and each block has 10 windows. For 8, 16, 24, 32, 48, 64, and 128 blocks, run 2,000 simulated tests, and print the range that holds the middle 95% of measured accuracies. What's the smallest number of blocks that pins accuracy within about ±5 points (a range 10 points wide or less)?

Need a hint?

For one simulated test of n blocks: p = rng.beta(8.5, 1.5, n), then right = rng.binomial(10, p), and the measured accuracy is right.sum() / (10 * n). Repeat 2,000 times and take np.percentile(results, [2.5, 97.5]).

Show solution

Going from 8 to 32 blocks halves the uncertainty, and halving it again takes about 128. That's the square-root rule: four times the data for twice the precision. Plan field tests in blocks across many people and places, because adding windows inside the same block barely helps.

#Challenge: Write the field-test plan for a wildlife camera

A camera trap classifies photos as animal or empty and only stores animal photos. Write a one-page field-test plan as a Markdown table plus a few sentences. Include:

  • the conditions you'll vary (at least time of day, weather, distance, and two camera mounting heights), and how many blocks per condition;
  • what the device logs for every photo, so you can score it later without guessing;
  • your pass targets, written before the test, for animal recall, empty-photo precision, and battery drain per day;
  • one feature-shift check you'll run on unlabeled photos to spot drift early (for example, average brightness by hour).
Need a hint?

Start from the gesture plan: truth logged on the device, transition windows dropped, results split by condition, bootstrap over blocks. For a camera, a "block" might be one night at one location. Exercise 6 tells you roughly how many you need.

What you'll learn

  • Compute average current from a duty cycle, and battery life from average current.
  • Explain why, at low duty cycles, sleep current matters more than the model's speed.
  • Compare the radio cost of sending raw sensor data with sending labels.
  • Say what on-device inference keeps private, and name four ways information still leaks.

A CR2032 coin cell holds roughly 220 mAh. Run a gesture remote at a steady 6 mA and the cell is flat in about a day and a half. Keep the same model and the same chip, but let it sleep between predictions so it averages 50 µA, and the same cell lasts around six months.

Nothing about the model changed. The difference is how much of each second the chip spends awake. This lesson does that arithmetic properly, then turns to the other reason TinyML runs on the device: the raw data never has to leave it. That protects more than you might expect, but less than people usually claim.

#Battery life is capacity divided by average current

A battery's capacity is a charge, measured in milliamp-hours (mAh): 220 mAh can supply 220 mA for one hour, 1 mA for 220 hours, or any other split. So:

battery life (hours) = capacity (mAh) ÷ average current (mA)

The hard part is the average. A TinyML device moves between states (asleep, sampling, running the model, using the radio), each with its own current and duration. The average is each state's current weighted by the share of time spent in it. Step through one 2-second cycle of a sensor that wakes every 2 seconds:

The chip sleeps 95% of the time, yet the 95 ms awake contributes almost all of the charge: 5 mA × 95 ms is 475, while sleep adds under 6. That's the first rule of power design: active time dominates until you make it tiny.

Where do these numbers come from? The nRF52840's product brief lists 6.4 mA for the radio transmitting at 0 dBm and 3.16 µA asleep in its "System ON" mode, with all RAM kept and a timer running to wake it (both measured with its DC/DC regulator at 3 V). The 5 mA for "sense + infer" is a planning figure for the CPU and sensor together; you replace it with a measurement.

#Duty cycling, and the floor that sleep current sets

The duty cycle is the fraction of time a device is awake. Average current is then:

average = duty × active current + (1 − duty) × sleep current

Lower the duty cycle and battery life climbs, but only until the sleep term takes over. Plot it:

At 100% awake, sleep current is irrelevant: about 2 days either way. At 0.1% awake, the 3 µA design lasts years and the 100 µA design stalls at a few months. Once a device is mostly asleep, cutting sleep current is worth more than any speed-up to the model.

That's why development boards are poor guides to battery life. A board like the Nano 33 BLE Sense keeps a power LED, a voltage regulator, and several sensors powered even when the chip sleeps, so it draws far more than the chip's 3 µA. Battery products use custom boards that switch peripherals off. Always measure the current of the hardware you'll actually ship.

The interrupt arrow is the second big lever. Many accelerometers and some microphones can watch for motion or sound on their own, drawing microamps, and wake the main chip only when something happens. The model then runs only on the moments that might matter.

#The radio is the expensive part

Pete Warden, who helped create TensorFlow Lite Micro at Google, put the rule simply: energy grows with how far you send the bits. Moving data a few millimeters to the CPU is cheap; moving it meters over a radio is expensive. Compare how much each design would have to transmit per day:

Streaming raw accelerometer data means 32 MB a day; raw audio, 2.8 GB. Sending labels is a few kilobytes, thousands of times less. Streaming audio also means the radio transmits all day, and at 6.4 mA the radio alone would flatten a coin cell in about a day and a half. For a battery-powered microphone, local inference isn't an optimization. It's the only design that works.

#What on-device inference protects

When the model runs on the device, the raw audio, images, and motion traces can be processed in RAM and thrown away. Nothing raw is transmitted, so there's nothing to intercept on the way, nothing piling up on a server to be breached, and no company holding hours of recordings from someone's home. Collecting only the data you need for a purpose has a name, data minimization, and privacy laws such as the EU's GDPR require it. On-device inference makes it the default.

#What still leaks

"The data never leaves the device" is a slogan, not a guarantee. Four leaks remain:

  1. The outputs themselves. A label is still information. A kitchen sound classifier that reports only "activity" with a timestamp still reveals when people wake, eat, and sleep, and when the house is empty.
  2. Metadata. Even with no content, the timing, size, and frequency of messages, plus the device's radio identity, show that something happened and roughly where.
  3. The device. Anyone holding the board may be able to read its flash through the debug port, unless the chip's readback protection is turned on. That exposes any stored clips or logs, and the model itself.
  4. Your development data. The recordings you collected to train and field-test the model are raw data. They need consent, secure storage, and deletion when the project ends.

The first leak is easiest to see. Here's one week of "activity" events from such a kitchen sensor, with only label and time sent:

From labels and timestamps alone you can read wake-up time, dinner time, bedtime, and the fact that nobody was home on Saturday. The fix is to send less: counts per day instead of timestamps, or nothing at all unless a user asks. The build-along designs exactly that.

⚠️ Watch out

Power and privacy mistakes that show up late

  1. Measuring battery life on a development board. LEDs, regulators, and sensors swamp the chip's sleep current. Measure the real hardware, or at least subtract what you can't ship.
  2. Forgetting serial debug output. A sketch that prints raw sensor values over Serial during development will happily do the same in the field. Remove raw-data prints before deployment.
  3. Treating labels as harmless. Timestamps on labels can reveal more than the label. Send the coarsest data the purpose needs.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1A device draws 4 mA awake and 2 µA asleep, and is awake 1% of the time. Roughly what is its average current?

  • That ignores the awake time, which dominates here.

  • 0.01 × 4 mA = 40 µA, plus 0.99 × 2 µA ≈ 2 µA, for about 42 µA.

  • That would be the average if it were awake half the time.

Show answer

B. 0.01 × 4 mA = 40 µA, plus 0.99 × 2 µA ≈ 2 µA, for about 42 µA.

2Your device draws 5 mA awake, is awake 0.05% of the time, and sleeps at 80 µA. Which change extends battery life most?

  • At 0.05% duty, active time contributes about 2.5 µA; halving it barely moves an 80 µA total.

  • Sleep is almost all of the average here, so it drops from about 82 µA to about 7.5 µA, roughly 10 times the life.

  • A bigger model makes active time longer, which can only shorten battery life.

Show answer

B. Sleep is almost all of the average here, so it drops from about 82 µA to about 7.5 µA, roughly 10 times the life.

3A doorbell runs a keyword spotter locally and sends only "doorbell pressed, 18:42". What can still leak?

  • The message itself carries information.

  • A log of times reveals routines and absences even without audio.

  • A label can't reconstruct audio; the risk is what the label and time reveal.

Show answer

B. A log of times reveals routines and absences even without audio.

Key takeaways

  • Battery life (hours) = capacity (mAh) ÷ average current (mA), and the average weights each state by its share of time.
  • Active time dominates until the duty cycle is small; after that, sleep current sets the ceiling.
  • Wake on interrupts so the model runs only when something might be happening.
  • Sending labels instead of raw data cuts radio traffic by thousands of times, which saves energy and protects privacy at once.
  • Outputs, metadata, physical access, and development data can all still leak. Send the coarsest data the purpose needs.

#Further reading

  • Why the future of machine learning is tiny (opens in a new tab) is Pete Warden's essay on radio versus computation costs and the sensor data nobody uses.
  • nRF52840 product brief (PDF) (opens in a new tab) lists the chip's sleep, radio, and memory figures on two pages.
  • Data minimization (opens in a new tab) covers the principle and where privacy laws require it.
