What you'll learn

  • Model a device as states with currents and durations, and compute charge per day.
  • Compare timer-driven and motion-triggered designs over a range of trigger rates.
  • Find which state dominates each design's energy, and what that means for optimization.
  • Write the code that builds each design's outgoing messages, and measure what they reveal.
  • Pick a design with numbers for both battery life and privacy.

A conservation group wants cameras on a forest trail to count deer, foxes, and a rare wildcat. The cameras run on two AA batteries, have a weak radio link to a base station, and someone can only reach them to change batteries a few times a year. The images will also include hikers, who never agreed to be photographed.

The camera uses the small image model you budgeted in module 5: about 300 ms per 96×96 image on a 64 MHz chip. It classifies each photo as animal, person, or empty. The question now is how to run it. Four designs are on the table:

Design When it takes a photo What it sends
A. Timer Every 10 seconds, all day A label for each animal photo
B. Motion, labels When a motion (PIR) sensor triggers A label and timestamp for each animal photo
C. Motion, cloud When motion triggers Every photo, classified at the base station
D. Motion, summary When motion triggers One message a day with counts per class

You'll build a calculator that gives each design a battery life and a privacy profile, and finish with a recommendation.

#Step 1: Put every state into numbers

Each state has a current and a duration. These are planning figures, not measurements: the chip's sleep current is from the nRF52840 product brief, and the rest are typical values for parts of this kind. Replace them with readings from a USB power meter or a current profiler once you have hardware.

Look at the sizes. One photo costs about 2.8 µAh, and one inference about 0.4 µAh. A day of sleeping costs about 1,500 µAh. Whether the camera's active work matters at all depends on how many times a day it happens.

#Step 2: Charge per day for each design

Write one function that returns a design's daily charge, split by category, for a given number of motion triggers per day.

At 50 triggers a day, the timer design lasts a little over two months. The motion-triggered designs last years on paper, because the camera sleeps nearly all the time. Treat any figure past a couple of years with suspicion: alkaline cells slowly self-discharge and lose capacity in the cold, so real life will be shorter. The ranking is what's reliable.

#Step 3: How busy is the trail?

Fifty triggers is a guess. A trail in summer with wind in the bushes might fire the PIR 500 times a day. Sweep it:

Three things stand out. Design A doesn't care about trail activity, because it photographs every 10 seconds anyway, and it's the worst by far. Design C falls fastest, because every trigger means 4 seconds of radio. And B and D sit almost on top of each other: sending a 0.2-second label for each animal costs very little compared with sleeping all day.

That last point matters. D doesn't win on battery. If you pick it, you pick it for another reason.

#Step 4: Where the charge goes

A bar per design, split by category, shows which state to attack first.

The biggest cost tells you what to optimize. For A, it's the camera: fix it by not taking photos nobody needs. For C, it's the radio. For B and D, it's sleep, and most of that is the PIR sensor's 50 µA. A lower-power PIR would extend B and D more than any change to the model. Speeding up inference would change nothing you could measure.

#Step 5: What each design sends, and what that reveals

Battery life can't separate B from D. Privacy can. Build the actual messages each design would send for one day of events, and measure them.

Now read each one as an outsider would:

  • C sends every photo, including about ten a day of hikers' faces, to a base station and probably a cloud server. That's the largest privacy harm and the largest radio cost.
  • B sends no images, but every message carries a time and a species. A record that the wildcat passes camera 7 at dawn most days is exactly what a poacher would want.
  • D sends one line per day: counts per species. People are dropped on the device and never counted, and no time of day leaves the camera.

Notice that "no images leave the device" was true for B and still wasn't enough. The label and the timestamp were the sensitive part.

#The finished calculator

Here's the planning tool as one script. Change the numbers at the top as you measure your hardware, and add designs as you think of them.

At 500 triggers a day, D still lasts years on paper, C drops to a few months, and A never makes it past ten weeks. D is the recommendation: tied for the best battery life, and the only design whose output is safe to publish.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Design B and design D last almost the same time. Why?

  • B sends a message per animal and D one per day, so their byte counts differ a lot.

  • About 1.5 mAh a day goes to sleep; 15 labels at about 1.7 µAh each add only about 2 percent.

  • Both run the model on every trigger; it's just cheap at 0.4 µAh per run.

Show answer

B. About 1.5 mAh a day goes to sleep; 15 labels at about 1.7 µAh each add only about 2 percent.

2You want B to last longer. Which change helps most?

  • The model uses about 1% of B's daily charge; halving it is invisible.

  • The PIR is most of the sleep current, and sleep is most of B's budget.

  • Radio is a small slice of B's budget, so batching saves little energy (though it does help privacy).

Show answer

B. The PIR is most of the sleep current, and sleep is most of B's budget.

3Design B sends no images. What is its main privacy risk?

  • The label plus time is what makes the data useful to someone with bad intentions.

  • B only sends labels; it never transmits images.

  • That's a reliability problem, not a privacy risk.

Show answer

A. The label plus time is what makes the data useful to someone with bad intentions.

Key takeaways

  • Write each design as states with current and duration, then compute charge per day; that one function answers most power questions.
  • Sweep the uncertain input (here, triggers per day) instead of trusting one guess.
  • Optimize the biggest slice. For motion-triggered devices that's usually sleep current, not the model.
  • Designs that tie on battery can differ sharply on privacy. Build the real messages and read them like an outsider.
  • On-device inference makes it possible to drop sensitive classes, such as people, before anything is stored or sent.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Add a design E that wakes on motion, classifies, and stores animal photos on an SD card for monthly collection. What's the privacy risk if a camera is stolen?
  • Add temperature: assume usable capacity drops to 60% in a winter month, and replot.
  • Add random noise to D's daily counts before sending, and see how much noise hides a single wildcat visit.

#Further reading

  • Duty cycle (opens in a new tab) covers the definition and the averaging behind every calculation in this lesson.
  • Differential privacy (opens in a new tab) explains the idea behind adding calibrated noise to counts, the extension suggested above.

m7-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Compute average current and battery life for always-on and duty-cycled devices.
  • Solve for the longest wake interval that still meets a battery-life target.
  • Decide which change (active current, active time, or sleep current) helps a given device most.
  • Check whether a radio can even carry a data stream before costing it.
  • Minimize a message to its purpose and measure what coarser timestamps hide.

The first four exercises are power; the last two are privacy. Every solution runs on its own. All currents are planning figures given in the task, so focus on the method.

#Warm-up

  1. A 220 mAh coin cell powers a device averaging 50 µA. How many days does it last?
  2. Two AA cells give 2,000 usable mAh. The device averages 1 mA. How many days?
Show solution
  1. 50 µA = 0.05 mA. 220 ÷ 0.05 = 4,400 hours = about 183 days.
  2. 2,000 ÷ 1 = 2,000 hours = about 83 days.

Always convert µA to mA before dividing, or your answer is off by a factor of a thousand.

#Exercise 1: The cost of always listening

A keyword spotter must hear every word, so its microphone never sleeps. The microphone draws 0.6 mA all the time. The CPU runs DSP and the model 25% of the time at 5 mA, and sleeps the rest at 3 µA. Compute the average current and the battery life on a 220 mAh coin cell and on 2,000 usable mAh of AA cells.

Need a hint?

Add the microphone's constant current to the CPU's duty-cycled average: 0.6 + 0.25 * 5 + 0.75 * 0.003.

Show solution

Always-on audio is expensive even with a tiny model, because the microphone and the constant processing never stop. That's why products use a low-power trigger first, such as a sound-level detector or a very small "is anyone speaking?" model, and wake the full keyword spotter only when it fires.

#Exercise 2: How long can it sleep?

A soil monitor wakes every T seconds, spends 120 ms at 5 mA sensing and classifying, and sleeps at 5 µA otherwise. It runs on a coin cell with 176 mAh usable (220 mAh at 80%). Find the smallest whole number T that makes it last at least 365 days, and plot battery life against T from 1 to 120 seconds.

Need a hint?

For a given T, the average is (5 * 0.12 + 0.005 * (T - 0.12)) / T in mA. Loop T upward from 1 and stop at the first one where 176 / avg / 24 >= 365.

Show solution

The curve flattens because, as T grows, the active part (0.6 / T mA) shrinks toward zero while the 5 µA sleep part stays. However long you sleep, this design can't beat 176 mAh ÷ 0.005 mA ≈ 1,467 days.

#Exercise 3: Which fix is worth it?

Two devices both draw 5 mA for 200 ms when awake and 10 µA asleep, with 176 mAh usable. One wakes every second (busy), the other every 60 seconds (idle). For each, compute how many times longer the battery lasts if you halve (a) the active current, (b) the active time, or (c) the sleep current.

Need a hint?

Write life(active_ma, active_s, period_s, sleep_ma) once, then call it with one value halved at a time and divide by the original.

Show solution

For the busy device, halving active current or time nearly doubles life, and sleep current is irrelevant. For the idle device, all three matter and none comes close to doubling, because active and sleep are similar in size. There's no universal "best optimization": compute it for your duty cycle before spending a week on one.

#Exercise 4: Can the radio even keep up?

A device's radio can send about 10 KB per second while drawing 8 mA. Compare three plans for a day: stream raw audio (16,000 samples per second, 2 bytes each), stream raw accelerometer data (62.5 Hz, 3 axes, 2 bytes), and send 300 labels of 20 bytes. For each, print the radio-on seconds needed per day and the radio's daily charge in mAh, and flag any plan that needs the radio on for more than 100% of the time.

Need a hint?

Radio seconds = bytes ÷ 10,240. Charge in mAh = 8 × seconds ÷ 3,600. Compare seconds with 86,400.

Show solution

Raw audio needs more than three seconds of airtime per second, so no amount of battery would save it. Raw accelerometer data fits, but at about 7 mAh a day the radio alone would empty a coin cell in about a month. Labels cost almost nothing. Check feasibility before cost: some designs fail on bandwidth before energy even comes into it.

#Exercise 5: Minimize a doorbell's message

A smart doorbell classifies sounds and visitors on the device. Its app shows one thing: how many visitors came each day. Here is what the firmware currently sends for every visitor:

Write minimize(msg) that returns only what the purpose needs, with the time coarsened to the date. Print both versions with their sizes as JSON. Then list, in a comment, one field you removed that a support engineer might argue for, and how you'd meet their need differently.

Need a hint?

The app needs a device to attribute the count to, a date, and the event. A random per-install ID can replace the serial and MAC. msg["timestamp"][:10] gives the date.

Show solution

The face crop, location, hardware identifiers, and minute-level time all go. Better still, the device could count visitors itself and send one message per day, which removes even the timing of individual visits.

#Exercise 6: How much does a timestamp reveal?

A bedroom motion sensor reports events for 14 days. An observer wants each day's wake-up time. The next cell makes the data. Compare three versions of what the device could send: (a) every event with its exact time, (b) counts per 4-hour block, (c) one count per day. For each, estimate wake-up time each day as best you can and print the average error in minutes, or say that it can't be estimated.

Need a hint?

For (a), the first event of each day is the estimate. For (b), the best you can do is the middle of the first block with any events. For (c), there's no time information at all.

Show solution

Exact times give the wake-up time to the minute, every day. Four-hour counts still say "an early riser" but blur the time by about three-quarters of an hour. A daily count says only how active the room was. Pick the coarsest level that still serves the product; if the app only shows daily activity, (c) is the honest choice.

#Challenge: A classroom noise monitor

A school wants a battery sensor in every classroom that classifies sound as quiet, talking, or loud and shows teachers a weekly chart. Write a half-page plan with numbers:

  • the duty cycle (does it need to listen continuously, or can it sample, say, 10 seconds every minute?), the average current, and the battery life on the cells you choose;
  • exactly what each message contains, how often it's sent, and who can see it;
  • one way the data could still be misused (for example, to judge a particular teacher), and the design choice that prevents it;
  • what happens to any audio, including during development and testing.
Need a hint?

Reuse the calculator from the build-along with a microphone state added. For privacy, ask what the weekly chart needs: probably counts per class per hour, aggregated across days, with no audio ever stored.

m8-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Pick a capstone device that fits your hardware, time, and interests.
  • Scope it in four sentences: who, what decision, cost of mistakes, smallest useful version.
  • Turn each need into a requirement with a number and a test.
  • Set up the design doc template and fill in its first two sections.
  • Check that every dataset you plan to use is yours or licensed for your use.

Here's the kind of sentence your capstone has to earn:

This wrist-worn gesture remote recognizes four gestures with at least 85% recall each on people it has never seen, uses under 80% of an nRF52840's flash and RAM, answers within 250 ms, runs 30 days on a coin cell, and transmits nothing but gesture names.

Every number in it needs a calculation or a measurement behind it. That's the capstone: a design doc for a small edge-AI device, where each claim about memory, speed, accuracy, power, and privacy points to evidence you produced. The modules gave you a tool for each claim. Now you put them in one place for one device.

#What you'll hand in

  1. A design doc (Markdown, Google Docs, or similar), using the template below.
  2. A Colab notebook with your budget, power, and test calculations, so a reader can rerun every number.
  3. Your model and data evidence: an Edge Impulse project (you can make it public or export it), or your notebook's training code, plus your field logs if you have hardware.
  4. A five-minute presentation, covered in the last lesson.

You can do the capstone on one of two tracks. On the hardware track you deploy to a real board: an Arduino Nano 33 BLE Sense, a micro:bit V2 with micro:bit CreateAI, or your phone connected to Edge Impulse as a sensor (on the Devices page, Connect a new device offers a mobile phone option). On the simulation track you train and test in Colab and Edge Impulse with recorded or simulated data, and budget against the nRF52840's published limits. Both tracks can earn full marks. What loses marks is presenting a simulated number as if it were measured.

#Five devices to choose from

Device Sensor and task The hard part Level
Gesture remote Accelerometer; 4 or 5 gestures Placement drift between people and wrists Starter
"Lights on / lights off" keyword spotter Microphone; 2 keywords plus unknown and noise Always-on listening power; other people's speech Intermediate
Machine-vibration monitor Accelerometer on a fan or washing machine; normal versus anomaly You have few or no examples of real faults Intermediate
Wildlife camera trap Camera, 96×96 grayscale; animal, person, empty RAM for images; hikers in photos; data licences Advanced
Sound alert for Deaf users (doorbell, smoke alarm) Microphone; event detection A missed alarm is dangerous; strict latency Advanced

Some notes to help you choose:

  • The gesture remote has the clearest path: everything from modules 5 to 7 applies directly, and you can record data with a Nano, a micro:bit, or a phone in an afternoon.
  • The keyword spotter forces the power question from module 7: you can't sleep through a word.
  • The vibration monitor is an anomaly-detection problem: you train on normal data and flag what doesn't fit. Simulated faults are fine if you say so.
  • The camera trap needs a stride-2 first layer or similar to fit in RAM (module 5) and an on-device policy for photos of people (module 7). Public camera-trap images, such as those on LILA BC, come with licences you must read and follow.
  • The sound alert is for people who rely on it, so recall and latency targets are strict. Your doc must say plainly that it does not replace a certified smoke alarm.

#Scope it in four sentences

Most capstone trouble starts with a vague goal ("detect gestures"). Answer these four questions in one sentence each before you collect any data:

  1. Who uses it, and where? Be specific about bodies, rooms, weather, and noise.
  2. What decision does it make, and how often? This sets the window, the hop, and the deadline.
  3. What does each kind of mistake cost? A missed event (false negative) and a false alarm (false positive) usually cost different things.
  4. What's the smallest version that would still be useful? That's your first milestone. Extras come after it works.

Here is the gesture remote, scoped:

  1. A student wears it on either wrist while presenting, standing or walking, indoors.
  2. Every 250 ms it decides between idle, next-slide (wave), previous-slide (snake), and pointer (updown).
  3. A false gesture jumps the slides, which is embarrassing and confusing, while a missed gesture just means waving again, so false positives cost more.
  4. Smallest useful version: two gestures (next and previous) plus idle, on one wrist.

Sentence 3 changes the design. Since false gestures cost more, the remote should require a high score before acting, and the doc should report precision for the action gestures as a headline target, not just recall.

#Turn each need into a number and a test

A requirement is only useful if you can check it. For each one, write the target and the test that will prove it:

For the gesture remote, the requirements table starts like this:

Requirement Target Evidence
Few false actions Precision ≥ 95% for wave and snake Field-test confusion matrix (module 6)
Recognises real gestures Recall ≥ 85% per gesture, every tester Field test split by tester
Feels responsive DSP + inference ≤ 125 ms, worst case Board timings from the log (module 6), estimate first (module 5)
Fits the board Flash and RAM ≤ 80% of 960 KB and 256 KB Budget table (module 5), then the compile report
Lasts a term ≥ 30 days on its battery Power model (module 7), then a measured current
Private by design Sends only gesture names; stores no raw motion Data-flow table and message examples (module 7)

Notice every target has a source. If you can't name the evidence, the requirement isn't finished.

#The design doc template

Copy this into your document and keep it as your table of contents. Sections 1 and 2 are due at the end of this lesson; the next lesson fills the rest milestone by milestone.

Section 11 matters more than it looks. A plan that names its own weak spots ("never tested on left wrists", "battery life is modeled, not measured") is far more useful, and scores higher, than one that claims everything works.

#Data you're allowed to use

You can use data you record yourself, with the agreement of everyone who appears in it, and public datasets whose licence allows your use. Before using any dataset you didn't make, write down three things in section 3: where it came from, its licence, and anything the licence requires (often, credit to the authors). Don't scrape images or audio from websites or videos. If you record other people's voices or faces, tell them what it's for, keep the raw files private, and delete them when the project ends.

#Milestones

The next lesson walks through each one with a starter notebook:

Check your understanding

3 questions

1A keyword spotter's team writes the requirement "works well in noisy rooms". What's missing?

  • "Well" and "noisy" can't be tested, so nobody can say whether the device meets it.

  • For example: recall ≥ 85% for each keyword at a stated noise level, from a field test in three real rooms.

  • The board belongs in the budget section, not in this requirement.

Show answer

B. For example: recall ≥ 85% for each keyword at a stated noise level, from a field test in three real rooms.

2For a smoke-alarm sound alert, which mistake should the targets guard hardest against?

  • A missed alarm could leave someone unaware of a fire, so recall is the headline target, even at the cost of some false alerts.

  • They're annoying, but far less harmful than missing a real alarm.

  • The costs aren't equal, and the targets should say so.

A. A missed alarm could leave someone unaware of a fire, so recall is the headline target, even at the cost of some false alerts.

3You're on the simulation track. Your battery life comes from the power model in module 7. How should the doc present it?

  • That hides that it's a model with assumed currents.

  • Honest labeling is what makes a simulated number useful, and it's what the rubric rewards.

  • An estimate with stated assumptions is still valuable evidence.

Key takeaways

  • The capstone is a design doc where every claim about accuracy, memory, latency, power, and privacy points to evidence.
  • Scope with four sentences: who and where, what decision how often, what mistakes cost, smallest useful version.
  • Each requirement needs a target number and a named test.
  • Simulated and measured numbers are both welcome, as long as each is labeled for what it is.
  • Use only data you recorded with consent or data licensed for your use, and record the licence.

What you'll learn

  • Keep every number in your design doc in one notebook that checks it against a target.
  • Plan how much data to record from a target number of windows.
  • Fill the budget, test, power, and privacy sections from the tools you built in modules 5 to 7.
  • Write the device firmware skeleton around run_classifier() with a decision threshold and a logging switch.
  • Produce a scorecard that labels every result as measured or estimated, and use it to decide what to do next.

A design doc goes stale the moment a number in it changes by hand. Change the model, and the flash figure in section 6, the latency in section 6, and the battery life in section 9 all move. If those numbers live in three places, one of them will be wrong when you present.

The fix is a single plan notebook. Every number goes in once, every check runs from it, and the doc's tables are copied from its output. This lesson builds that notebook for the gesture remote from the last lesson, one milestone at a time. You'll then swap in your own device.

#Milestone 1: Spec, targets, and a check function

Copy your four scoping sentences into the doc, then put the requirements table's targets into code. The check() function records each result with its source and whether it was measured or estimated. That label is what keeps the simulation track honest.

Nothing is checked yet. The point of writing targets first is that you can't quietly move them after seeing results.

#Milestone 2: Plan the data and the window

The window and hop come from your scoping sentence about decisions. How much to record comes from how many windows you want. A recording of d seconds, cut into windows of w seconds every h seconds, gives (d − w) / h + 1 windows, but overlapping windows from the same recording are not independent examples. Plan by sessions (people and placements) first, then minutes.

Hold out whole people, not random windows, for the test set. If one person's windows are in both training and test, the test score measures how well the model remembers that person.

In the doc's section 3, list who recorded data, that they agreed, and where the files are kept. In Edge Impulse, the Data acquisition page shows your samples and the train/test split.

#Milestone 3: Train two candidates and fill the budget

Train at least two models (in Edge Impulse, or in Colab as in module 5), and run profile() from the build-along in module 5 on each. Paste its output into MODEL. The firmware figures are placeholders until you compile; on the hardware track, replace them with the Arduino IDE's "Sketch uses … bytes" and "Global variables use … bytes" lines.

Record in section 5 why you chose this candidate over the other. "It passed the budget with room to spare and matched the CNN's accuracy on held-out people" is a good reason. "It was the first one I tried" is not.

#Milestone 4: Deploy, run the parity check, and write the firmware

In Edge Impulse Studio, open Deployment, choose Arduino library, pick Quantized (int8) under the model optimizations, note the estimated latency, RAM, and flash, and click Build. Install the .zip with Sketch › Include Library › Add .ZIP Library…, run the static_buffer example on a few test samples, and record the result.

On the simulation track, do the deployment build in Studio anyway (it's free) and record the estimates; skip the board run and say so.

Then write the product firmware. It's the field logger from module 6 with three changes: it acts on gestures, it only acts when the top score clears a threshold (because false actions cost more than misses), and logging is a switch you turn off before shipping.

#if FIELD_LOG removes the logging code entirely when set to 0, so no motion-derived data goes out over USB in the shipped device. That's a privacy decision written into the build, and section 10 of your doc should mention it.

#Milestone 5: Test, then paste the results in

Run the field test from module 6: at least three people, both wrists, labeled blocks, transition windows dropped. Paste the confusion matrix from field_report.py here. On the simulation track, test on simulated "field" data with a stated change, such as tilt, and label it as simulated.

Recall passes for every gesture, but precision for the three action gestures falls short of 95%. Users would see a wrong slide change roughly once every ten actions. That's a real finding, and it's exactly what the threshold in the firmware is for.

#Milestone 6: Power, privacy, and the decision

Fill in the power model from module 7 with this device's states. A gesture remote can't sleep through gestures, so its accelerometer stays on and the CPU wakes for every sample.

The battery estimate fails: about 18 days on a coin cell against a 30-day target, with the always-on accelerometer the largest part. That gives you three honest options for the doc: a bigger battery (a small rechargeable cell), a smarter design (stop classifying after a minute of idle and wake on motion), or a revised target. Write which you chose and why.

Now draw the scorecard. Each bar is the result divided by its target, flipped where lower is better, so anything at or past 1.0 passes. Hatched bars are estimates.

The decision is revise, with a to-do list written by the notebook: raise ACT_THRESHOLD and re-measure precision (accepting some recall loss), fix the battery plan, and turn the estimated budget numbers into measurements by compiling the sketch.

Here is the whole plan as one file to copy into Colab and adapt. Replace every number with yours, keep the kind label honest, and paste its printed output into your doc.

3 questions

  • On the simulation track especially, the label is what makes the plan trustworthy.

  • Estimates can pass or fail; the label says how much to trust them.

2Recall passes but action precision fails. Which firmware change is the direct response?

  • A higher threshold suppresses low-confidence actions, trading some recall for precision.

  • That would let even more uncertain predictions act, lowering precision further.

  • Logging doesn't change predictions; it only affects what's printed.

3Why plan data by people and placements rather than just total minutes?

  • It has no such rule.

  • Drift comes from people and placement; the plan has to cover them, and the test set should hold out whole people.

  • Training data never goes on the device.

Key takeaways

  • Put every number in one plan notebook, check it against a target, and copy the doc's tables from its output.
  • Label every result as measured, estimated, or a design choice.
  • Plan data by people and placements, and hold out whole people for testing.
  • Build the firmware around run_classifier() with a decision threshold and a compile-time logging switch.
  • A FAIL is a normal outcome. The plan's job is to make the next step obvious.

What you'll learn

  • Complete a final test pass that covers accuracy, timing, power, privacy, and failure behavior.
  • Tune a decision threshold from field data and handle the case where no threshold meets every target.
  • Polish the design doc so every number has a source and every estimate is labeled.
  • Present the plan in five minutes, with evidence a reviewer can check.
  • Grade your own work against the rubric and plan what to learn next.

Picture the review. Someone who has never seen your device reads the doc for ten minutes, then asks three questions: How do you know that number? What didn't you test? What result would make you stop? A strong capstone has answers to all three already written down. This lesson gets you there.

#The final test pass

By now you have budget estimates, a parity check, and field results. Before you present, run the tests that only make sense on a nearly finished design. On the simulation track, do the ones you can and list the rest under Risks and limits.

Test What it proves Pass target (gesture remote) Evidence
Unseen-person test Accuracy holds for people not in training Recall ≥ 85% for each held-out person Field log per person
New-place test Accuracy holds in a new environment Within 5 points of the main field test Field log from the new place
Compile report The budget estimate was right Flash and RAM ≤ 80% Arduino IDE "Sketch uses" and "Global variables use" lines
Soak test It runs for hours without crashing or slowing 4 hours, no resets, latency p99 unchanged Log with timestamps
Current measurement The power model's biggest line is right Measured average within 30% of the model USB power meter or current profiler reading
Privacy test Only what the data-flow table says leaves the device With FIELD_LOG 0, nothing but labels is sent A Bluetooth scanner app or serial capture
Failure test It fails safely Sensor unplugged or low battery: no false actions Bench notes

The privacy test deserves a word. Don't trust the code to do what you think it does; watch what actually goes out. A free Bluetooth scanner app on a phone can show what the device sends, and the Serial Monitor shows what goes over USB.

#Tune the threshold, and face the trade-off

The last lesson ended with action precision below its 95% target and a firmware threshold to tune. Precision and recall pull against each other: raising the threshold blocks more wrong actions but also more right ones. The field log has a score for every window, so you can test every threshold without going back into the field.

The next cell rebuilds a log with scores that matches the confusion matrix from the last lesson. Use your own field_*.csv files in its place.

For each threshold, an action happens only when the top label is an action gesture and its score clears the threshold. Precision counts how many actions were right; recall counts how many real gestures led to the right action.

No threshold meets both targets. At 0.65, precision reaches about 97%, but updown's recall drops to about 83%. This happens in real projects, and the doc has to make a call rather than hide it. Go back to your scoping sentences: for the gesture remote, a false action costs more than a missed one. So the defensible decision is to set the threshold to 0.65, keep the precision target, and lower the recall target to 80% with that reason written next to it, while listing "more wrist-worn updown data" as the next improvement. Changing a target after seeing results is only acceptable when you say so openly and tie it to a reason you wrote down before testing.

#Polish the doc

Before presenting, read the doc once with each of these questions:

  • Does every number have a source? A calculation in the notebook, a measurement with a date, or a cited datasheet. "About 5 mA" with no source is not evidence.
  • Is every estimate labeled? Use the scorecard's measured, estimated, and design labels in your tables.
  • Are units and data types attached? "218 KB (int8 weights)", not "218".
  • Does section 11 name real weaknesses? Untested conditions, modeled-not-measured numbers, small numbers of testers.
  • Does section 12 make a decision? Ship, revise, or stop, with the numbers that decide it.
  • Can someone rerun it? Share the notebook and say where the data is (or why it can't be shared).

Then write a one-page summary at the top: the device in one sentence, the scorecard chart, the three most important results, and the decision.

#Present it in five minutes

  • Spend the most time on evidence. One confusion matrix and the scorecard beat ten slides of architecture.
  • If you have hardware, show a 20-second video of the device working, including one mistake. It's more convincing than a perfect demo.
  • Say "estimated" and "measured" out loud when you quote a number.
  • End on the decision, not on "thank you". "We'd ship after one more round of wrist data, because…" is a strong last line.

#The rubric

Criterion Points Excellent Developing
Problem and requirements 10 Four scoping sentences; every requirement has a target and a named test Goals are vague or untestable
Data and rights 10 Sources, amounts, consent, and licences recorded; test set holds out whole people or places Unclear where data came from, or test data overlaps training
Model and budget 15 Two or more candidates compared; flash, RAM, and latency budgeted against a named board with headroom One model, no budget, or model size only
Deployment and parity 10 Edge Impulse build recorded with int8/float32 choice; parity check done or its absence explained Deployment described vaguely
Testing and accuracy 20 Test ladder followed; per-class and per-condition results; uncertainty from blocks; threshold tuned Single accuracy number from the training tool
Power 10 States, currents, duty cycle, and battery life, with the biggest cost identified and addressed No power analysis, or an unexplained figure
Privacy 15 Data-flow table; minimized messages; remaining leaks named with mitigations "Data stays on the device" with no analysis
Honesty and limits 10 Every number labeled measured or estimated; real weaknesses listed; a clear decision Simulated results presented as measured

The total is 100. Notice that honesty is graded on its own and also runs through every other row. A simulation-track plan that labels everything clearly can outscore a hardware plan that overclaims.

#Reflect

Write a short paragraph for each before you hand in:

  1. Which number surprised you most when you measured or computed it, and what had you assumed instead?
  2. Which limit (flash, RAM, latency, accuracy, power, or privacy) shaped your design most? Would that change on a different board?
  3. What would you test next with one more week and one more person to help?
  4. Who could be harmed if this device were deployed widely with its current weaknesses, and what would you change first?
